fallacies.name: A priori argument
fallacies.summary: Selecting reasons only to defend a predetermined conclusion while insulating it from contrary evidence.
fallacies.body: Selecting reasons only to defend a predetermined conclusion while insulating it from contrary evidence. In some rhetoric catalogs this label describes dogmatic rationalization, rather than legitimate reasoning independent of experience. The defect is treating the conclusion as immune to the evidence that is supposedly being assessed.

examples.text: I already know this treatment always works, so any failed trial must have been designed incorrectly.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A conclusion is held fixed, and every contrary result is dismissed without an independently supported reason.
doesNotCountWhen: A priori reasoning in mathematics or philosophy is not fallacious merely because it does not begin with an experiment.

fallacies.name: Abusive ad hominem
fallacies.summary: The argument rejects a claim by attacking its proponent's character instead of addressing the claim.
fallacies.body: The argument rejects a claim by attacking its proponent's character instead of addressing the claim. A person's faults do not by themselves make the person's proposition false.

examples.text: Lena says the bridge design fails a load test, but Lena is dishonest, so the design is safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response targets the speaker's character while leaving the stated evidence unanswered.
doesNotCountWhen: Relevant evidence about a speaker's reliability counts when it directly bears on testimony or motive and is not treated as a refutation by itself.

fallacies.name: Accent fallacy
fallacies.summary: The argument changes a sentence's meaning by shifting emphasis or stress between words.
fallacies.body: The argument changes a sentence's meaning by shifting emphasis or stress between words. Spoken emphasis can create a different proposition from the one actually asserted or written without that emphasis.

examples.text: The contract says the tenant must pay rent on time, and the landlord stresses must to claim that late payment is never excusable under any circumstance.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A disputed conclusion depends on an unmarked or misleading change in word stress or typographical emphasis.
doesNotCountWhen: Clarifying intended emphasis or distinguishing genuinely different readings is not fallacious.

fallacies.name: Accident
fallacies.summary: The argument applies a general rule to an exceptional case where its usual conditions do not hold.
fallacies.body: The argument applies a general rule to an exceptional case where its usual conditions do not hold. A rule framed for ordinary cases can mislead when a special circumstance defeats its purpose or scope.

examples.text: One should return borrowed property, so a doctor must return a delirious patient's loaded pistol immediately.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A universal or broad rule is applied without accounting for a relevant exception recognized by the rule's purpose.
doesNotCountWhen: Applying a rule to a case that satisfies its stated conditions and lacks a relevant exception is legitimate.

fallacies.name: Ad fidentia
fallacies.summary: The argument treats confidence or self-assurance as evidence that a claim is true.
fallacies.body: The argument treats confidence or self-assurance as evidence that a claim is true. Confidence is a psychological state and does not establish the proposition's evidential support.

examples.text: Mira announces confidently that the drug cures cancer, so the drug must work.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The claim's main support is the advocate's certainty, assertive tone, or lack of hesitation.
doesNotCountWhen: Confidence can appropriately communicate a conclusion when independent evidence supplies its support.

fallacies.name: Ad hoc rescue
fallacies.summary: The argument adds an unsupported special assumption solely to protect a claim from a counterexample.
fallacies.body: The argument adds an unsupported special assumption solely to protect a claim from a counterexample. A rescue assumption that has no independent support reduces testability rather than explaining the evidence.

examples.text: Every raven is black; this white bird is a raven that turns white only when observed, so the rule remains true.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An exception is introduced after disconfirmation and is tailored to avoid the observed problem.
doesNotCountWhen: An independently motivated auxiliary hypothesis that makes new testable predictions is not merely an ad hoc rescue.

fallacies.name: Affirmative conclusion from a negative premise
fallacies.summary: The syllogistic inference draws an affirmative conclusion from at least one negative premise.
fallacies.body: The syllogistic inference draws an affirmative conclusion from at least one negative premise. In standard categorical syllogisms a negative premise requires a negative conclusion because it denies a predicate relation.

examples.text: No poets are engineers, and some engineers are musicians, so some musicians are poets.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A categorical argument has a negative premise but concludes that a subject belongs affirmatively to a class without valid connecting structure.
doesNotCountWhen: An affirmative conclusion may follow from premises that are not a standard categorical syllogism or that include additional valid premises.

fallacies.name: Affirming a disjunct
fallacies.summary: Inferring that one alternative is false because the other is true, although both could be true.
fallacies.body: Inferring that one alternative is false because the other is true, although both could be true. An inclusive disjunction permits both alternatives; affirming one does not exclude the other.

examples.text: The sensor uses USB power or battery power. It uses USB power, so it cannot also use battery power.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The form is P ∨ Q; P; therefore ¬Q, or its symmetric form, without an exclusivity premise.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is valid when the alternatives are known to be mutually exclusive.

fallacies.name: Affirming the consequent
fallacies.summary: The argument infers the antecedent from a conditional and its consequent.
fallacies.body: The argument infers the antecedent from a conditional and its consequent. P → Q rules out P being true while Q is false, but it permits Q to be true while P is false; no causal interpretation is required.

examples.text: If the alarm is armed, the light is on; the light is on, so the alarm is armed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The form is If A then B; B; therefore A, with no premise excluding other causes of B.
doesNotCountWhen: The conclusion follows if an additional justified premise establishes Q → P; a tentative inference to the best explanation also has a different standard.

fallacies.name: Alleged certainty
fallacies.summary: The argument presents a contested or poorly supported conclusion as unquestionably certain.
fallacies.body: The argument presents a contested or poorly supported conclusion as unquestionably certain. Stating certainty does not remove uncertainty from the evidence or justify an absolute conclusion.

examples.text: There is no doubt that this eyewitness account proves the suspect was present.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The wording suppresses qualification despite incomplete, disputed, or probabilistic support.
doesNotCountWhen: A conclusion can properly be stated as certain when deductively entailed by true premises or established beyond reasonable doubt by the context.

fallacies.name: Alphabet soup
fallacies.summary: The argument uses unexplained acronyms or technical abbreviations to create an appearance of expertise in place of reasons.
fallacies.body: The argument uses unexplained acronyms or technical abbreviations to create an appearance of expertise in place of reasons. Opaque terminology can obscure missing premises and prevent evaluation of the actual claim.

examples.text: Our QRM-AXL protocol is superior because its NPV and K-factor demonstrate a high SFI.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion relies on jargon or strings of initials that are not defined or connected to evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Specialist abbreviations are legitimate when defined, relevant, and used to state inspectable evidence or calculations.

fallacies.name: Alternative advance
fallacies.summary: The argument answers criticism by introducing an alternative claim without showing that the alternative is supported or relevant.
fallacies.body: The argument answers criticism by introducing an alternative claim without showing that the alternative is supported or relevant. Merely proposing another possibility does not establish the preferred conclusion or defeat the objection.

examples.text: The audit found unexplained payments, but perhaps they were gifts, so the accounts are clean.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A bare alternative is offered as though it resolves evidence against the original claim.
doesNotCountWhen: An alternative explanation is legitimate when comparative evidence supports it or when it is offered only as a hypothesis.

fallacies.name: Alternative truth
fallacies.summary: Presenting an incompatible factual assertion as an equally valid truth without resolving the evidential conflict.
fallacies.body: Presenting an incompatible factual assertion as an equally valid truth without resolving the evidential conflict. The nonstandard rhetoric label concerns substituting a preferred account for a checkable fact. Disagreement about values or interpretation must be distinguished from mutually incompatible assertions about the same event.

examples.text: The attendance register lists 80 people, but our alternative truth is that 800 attended, so no correction is needed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Incompatible claims about the same checkable matter are insulated from comparison by labeling each true.
doesNotCountWhen: Different estimates can both be reasonable when uncertainty, scope, or measurement methods are explicitly distinguished.

fallacies.name: Ambiguity fallacy
fallacies.summary: The argument treats a word or phrase with multiple meanings as though it had one meaning throughout.
fallacies.body: The argument treats a word or phrase with multiple meanings as though it had one meaning throughout. An equivocation changes the proposition being supported while preserving the same wording.

examples.text: A bank is beside a river; money is in a bank; therefore money is beside a river.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A key term shifts sense between premises or between a premise and the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: Using a word in one stable sense or explicitly distinguishing its senses is not fallacious.

fallacies.name: Amphiboly
fallacies.summary: The argument exploits grammatical ambiguity in a sentence's structure or attachment.
fallacies.body: The argument exploits grammatical ambiguity in a sentence's structure or attachment. A syntactically ambiguous statement can support incompatible readings, so one reading cannot be selected without justification.

examples.text: The notice says employees who use the elevator must wear helmets, so employees wearing helmets may use the elevator.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion depends on rearranging or assuming a grammatical attachment not fixed by the wording.
doesNotCountWhen: Resolving an ambiguity by context or rewriting the sentence before reasoning is legitimate.

fallacies.name: Anecdotal fallacy
fallacies.summary: The argument generalizes or establishes a causal claim from an isolated personal story.
fallacies.body: The argument generalizes or establishes a causal claim from an isolated personal story. A vivid anecdote is not necessarily representative and does not control confounding causes.

examples.text: My uncle smoked until ninety, so smoking does not cause serious disease.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A single or few informal cases are used to override systematic evidence or support a broad population claim.
doesNotCountWhen: An anecdote is relevant as an illustration, a report requiring investigation, or evidence about that person's experience.

fallacies.name: Anonymous authority
fallacies.summary: The argument relies on an unnamed authority whose identity and competence cannot be checked.
fallacies.body: The argument relies on an unnamed authority whose identity and competence cannot be checked. An unverifiable attribution cannot independently establish the authority's expertise or the claimed fact.

examples.text: A leading scientist says the bridge is safe, so no inspection is needed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The authority is anonymous and the claim's credibility rests on the inaccessible attribution.
doesNotCountWhen: Anonymous testimony can be considered provisionally when identity must be protected and corroboration or reasons are supplied.

fallacies.name: Anthropomorphic fallacy
fallacies.summary: The argument projects human intentions, emotions, or purposes onto nonhuman things without evidence.
fallacies.body: The argument projects human intentions, emotions, or purposes onto nonhuman things without evidence. Human-like language does not show that an organism, object, or process has the corresponding mental state.

examples.text: The river is angry at the town because it flooded the streets.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A nonhuman event is explained by assigning it an unsupported human motive or feeling.
doesNotCountWhen: Anthropomorphic language is harmless metaphor or a supported claim about an animal's mental state when evidence warrants it.

fallacies.name: Appeal to accomplishment
fallacies.summary: The argument treats a person's success in one area as proof that the person's current claim is true.
fallacies.body: The argument treats a person's success in one area as proof that the person's current claim is true. Achievement does not automatically transfer expertise or establish the relevant proposition.

examples.text: The champion runner says this tax policy will reduce inflation, so it will reduce inflation.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker's past accomplishment is offered instead of domain-relevant evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: An accomplishment is relevant when it directly demonstrates competence for the claim at issue.

fallacies.name: Appeal to age
fallacies.summary: The argument treats a claim as true or false because it is old or new in age.
fallacies.body: The argument treats a claim as true or false because it is old or new in age. Age alone neither validates a tradition nor refutes a longstanding result.

examples.text: This medical treatment is ancient, so it must be effective.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion follows solely from the claim's historical age rather than evidence of effectiveness.
doesNotCountWhen: Historical duration can be relevant evidence about persistence or provenance when not used as proof by itself.

fallacies.name: Appeal to anger
fallacies.summary: The argument uses anger to pressure acceptance instead of providing relevant reasons.
fallacies.body: The argument uses anger to pressure acceptance instead of providing relevant reasons. Emotional intensity does not determine whether the conclusion follows from the evidence.

examples.text: You should approve this zoning request because I am furious that anyone would question my family.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Anger or indignation is presented as the reason the audience must accept the claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Anger can appropriately signal urgency or moral concern while independent reasons support the conclusion.

fallacies.name: Appeal to celebrity
fallacies.summary: The argument treats a celebrity's endorsement as proof of a claim outside the celebrity's demonstrated expertise.
fallacies.body: The argument treats a celebrity's endorsement as proof of a claim outside the celebrity's demonstrated expertise. Fame does not supply competence or evidence in the relevant subject.

examples.text: A famous actor endorses this investment fund, so it cannot lose money.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The celebrity's status is the principal support for the substantive conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A celebrity's statement may be evidence of the celebrity's preference or relevant expertise if independently established.

fallacies.name: Appeal to closure
fallacies.summary: The argument accepts a conclusion merely because it ends uncertainty or discomfort.
fallacies.body: The argument accepts a conclusion merely because it ends uncertainty or discomfort. Psychological relief does not make an explanation true or an investigation complete.

examples.text: We should declare the missing hiker dead now because the family needs closure.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The need to end suspense or emotional distress is treated as evidence for the factual conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: Closure may justify a practical decision or ritual without being presented as proof of the underlying fact.

fallacies.name: Appeal to coincidence
fallacies.summary: The argument infers a meaningful connection from events occurring together by chance.
fallacies.body: The argument infers a meaningful connection from events occurring together by chance. Coincidence is possible, and temporal or thematic coincidence alone does not establish a causal or intentional link.

examples.text: The stock rose after I wore my lucky watch, so the watch caused the rise.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion depends only on an unusual or timely coincidence without causal evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A coincidence can prompt an investigation or support a claim when probability and additional evidence make chance implausible.

fallacies.name: Appeal to common belief
fallacies.summary: The argument treats widespread belief as proof that the belief is true.
fallacies.body: The argument treats widespread belief as proof that the belief is true. Many people can share a false belief through error, conformity, or common misinformation.

examples.text: Most citizens believe the defendant is guilty, so the defendant is guilty.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Popularity of belief is used as the decisive warrant for its truth.
doesNotCountWhen: A common belief can be evidence of social attitudes or a relevant probabilistic indicator when supported by independent reasons.

fallacies.name: Appeal to common folk
fallacies.summary: The argument treats ordinary people's supposed viewpoint as inherently more reliable than expert or contrary evidence.
fallacies.body: The argument treats ordinary people's supposed viewpoint as inherently more reliable than expert or contrary evidence. Being ordinary does not guarantee accuracy, and expertise is not refuted by social identity.

examples.text: People like us know vaccines are dangerous, so epidemiologists are wrong.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker invokes an idealized common person to dismiss evidence without examining it.
doesNotCountWhen: Public experience is relevant to ordinary observations and values when it is not treated as infallible.

fallacies.name: Appeal to common practice
fallacies.summary: The argument concludes that a practice is right or safe because people commonly do it.
fallacies.body: The argument concludes that a practice is right or safe because people commonly do it. Frequency reflects habit or incentives, not moral correctness or factual reliability.

examples.text: Everyone in the industry hides these fees, so hiding them is acceptable.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The prevalence of a practice is offered as its justification.
doesNotCountWhen: Common practice can be relevant evidence about convention or feasibility, but not by itself about morality or truth.

fallacies.name: Appeal to common sense
fallacies.summary: The argument treats an intuition labeled common sense as sufficient proof against analysis or evidence.
fallacies.body: The argument treats an intuition labeled common sense as sufficient proof against analysis or evidence. What seems obvious varies with experience and can be systematically mistaken.

examples.text: Common sense says heavier objects fall faster, so the measurements must be wrong.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The claim relies on an asserted shared intuition rather than testable reasons.
doesNotCountWhen: Common-sense judgment is legitimate as a defeasible starting point when consistent with evidence and open to correction.

fallacies.name: Appeal to complexity
fallacies.summary: The argument treats a complicated explanation as more credible merely because the issue seems complicated.
fallacies.body: The argument treats a complicated explanation as more credible merely because the issue seems complicated. Complexity can increase opportunities for error and does not substitute for explanatory support.

examples.text: The budget must be accurate because its model has thousands of variables.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The number of components or technical details is used as the main evidence of correctness.
doesNotCountWhen: Necessary complexity is legitimate when the phenomenon and evidence require it and the model makes successful predictions.

fallacies.name: Appeal to consequences
fallacies.summary: The argument judges a proposition's truth solely by whether its consequences would be desirable or undesirable.
fallacies.body: The argument judges a proposition's truth solely by whether its consequences would be desirable or undesirable. A belief's practical or emotional consequences do not determine the facts, though they may affect decisions.

examples.text: If climate change is real, coastal towns must relocate, so climate change is not real.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion about truth is inferred from feared or welcomed consequences rather than evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Consequences are legitimate grounds for choosing an action or assessing a policy, not for establishing a factual proposition.

fallacies.name: Appeal to desperation
fallacies.summary: The argument uses an urgent need or lack of alternatives as support for a conclusion.
fallacies.body: The argument uses an urgent need or lack of alternatives as support for a conclusion. Desperation can explain a choice but does not make the chosen belief or claim true.

examples.text: We have no other suspect, so the arrested person must be the thief.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The absence of a usable alternative is treated as evidence sufficient for the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: Urgency may justify a provisional action under a decision rule while the conclusion remains qualified.

fallacies.name: Appeal to emotion
fallacies.summary: The argument substitutes an emotional reaction for relevant support.
fallacies.body: The argument substitutes an emotional reaction for relevant support. Feeling sympathy, disgust, pride, or outrage does not establish the truth of the asserted conclusion.

examples.text: The proposal must be approved because its opponents make me feel ashamed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An emotion is offered as the decisive reason for a factual or normative conclusion without further argument.
doesNotCountWhen: Emotion can be relevant evidence about preferences or moral salience when combined with reasons appropriate to the issue.

fallacies.name: Appeal to equality
fallacies.summary: The argument assumes that equal treatment requires identical treatment despite relevant differences.
fallacies.body: The argument assumes that equal treatment requires identical treatment despite relevant differences. Fairness can require distinctions when circumstances, rights, or needs differ.

examples.text: Every patient must receive the same dose because treating patients equally means identical doses.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument invokes equality while ignoring medically relevant differences.
doesNotCountWhen: Equal treatment is sound when the cases are relevantly alike or when an equal rule is independently justified.

fallacies.name: Appeal to extremes
fallacies.summary: The argument rejects a moderate position by associating it with an extreme or by arguing from an extreme case alone.
fallacies.body: The argument rejects a moderate position by associating it with an extreme or by arguing from an extreme case alone. An extreme case does not determine the ordinary case, and a moderate claim need not share an extreme's assumptions.

examples.text: If we permit one late assignment, soon students will demand no deadlines, so no extensions are ever justified.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion follows through an unsupported slide to an extreme outcome or an unrepresentative edge case.
doesNotCountWhen: Extreme cases can test a rule's limits or reveal a real implication when the intermediate steps are supported.

fallacies.name: Appeal to faith
fallacies.summary: The argument treats faith or commitment as sufficient evidence for a proposition.
fallacies.body: The argument treats faith or commitment as sufficient evidence for a proposition. Personal conviction does not establish a claim for people who do not share the commitment.

examples.text: I believe the prophecy is true by faith, so no evidence against it matters.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Faith is offered as a warrant that immunizes the conclusion from examination.
doesNotCountWhen: Faith can guide personal commitment or operate within a stated religious framework without being presented as public proof.

fallacies.name: Appeal to false authority
fallacies.summary: The argument relies on a purported authority who lacks the relevant expertise or whose authority is fabricated.
fallacies.body: The argument relies on a purported authority who lacks the relevant expertise or whose authority is fabricated. An authority outside the field cannot substitute for evidence about the field's subject matter.

examples.text: A television astrologer says the bridge is structurally sound, so engineers need not inspect it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The cited authority is irrelevant, unqualified, or falsely represented as expert on the claim.
doesNotCountWhen: An authority is appropriate when the person is competent in the relevant domain and the claim is within that competence.

fallacies.name: Appeal to fear
fallacies.summary: The argument uses fear of harm or punishment as support for accepting a conclusion.
fallacies.body: The argument uses fear of harm or punishment as support for accepting a conclusion. A threatened consequence does not make the proposition true, though it may affect prudential choices.

examples.text: Believe that the accused is guilty, or the criminal will escape and attack your family.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Fear is used in place of evidence that the accused is guilty.
doesNotCountWhen: Fear can be relevant to risk assessment or a conditional decision when the threatened outcome is supported and the claim is not thereby proved.

fallacies.name: Appeal to flattery
fallacies.summary: The argument seeks agreement by praising the audience rather than supporting the conclusion.
fallacies.body: The argument seeks agreement by praising the audience rather than supporting the conclusion. Praise may influence compliance but does not establish the proposition.

examples.text: A discerning investor like you will obviously buy this untested bond.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The audience's supposed intelligence, virtue, or status is used as the principal reason to agree.
doesNotCountWhen: Compliments are harmless when unrelated to the reasoning and no conclusion is supported by them.

fallacies.name: Appeal to force
fallacies.summary: The argument threatens harm to secure acceptance of a conclusion.
fallacies.body: The argument threatens harm to secure acceptance of a conclusion. Coercion can produce compliance but cannot make the proposition true.

examples.text: Sign this report saying the machine passed, or you will lose your job.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A threat replaces reasons for the asserted claim or demanded judgment.
doesNotCountWhen: Force may be relevant to explaining behavior or establishing that a threat exists, but not to proving the threatened proposition.

fallacies.name: Appeal to heaven
fallacies.summary: The argument ends a dispute by appealing to divine approval or a supernatural authority without shared grounds.
fallacies.body: The argument ends a dispute by appealing to divine approval or a supernatural authority without shared grounds. An asserted divine endorsement is not independently available as evidence in a public argument.

examples.text: The policy is just because heaven approves it, and anyone who disagrees rejects heaven.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion depends on an unverified appeal to divine will rather than accessible reasons.
doesNotCountWhen: A theological argument can be valid within accepted premises when the premises and interpretive standards are explicitly shared.

fallacies.name: Appeal to inappropriate authority
fallacies.summary: The argument cites a genuine authority whose expertise or institutional role does not cover the conclusion.
fallacies.body: The argument cites a genuine authority whose expertise or institutional role does not cover the conclusion. Expertise is domain-specific and cannot be transferred merely by prestige.

examples.text: A Nobel physicist says this ancient-language translation is correct, so the translation is correct.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The cited authority is respected but lacks relevant competence for the claim.
doesNotCountWhen: The authority is appropriate when the claim falls within the person's demonstrated expertise and the source is accurately represented.

fallacies.name: Appeal to intuition
fallacies.summary: The argument treats a spontaneous feeling of obviousness as sufficient evidence.
fallacies.body: The argument treats a spontaneous feeling of obviousness as sufficient evidence. Intuitions can be useful heuristics but are affected by framing, bias, and unfamiliarity.

examples.text: The algorithm is unfair because it feels unfair to me, so the audit data can be ignored.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion rests on an unexamined personal impression instead of relevant reasons.
doesNotCountWhen: Intuition can guide hypothesis formation or reflect trained judgment when checked against evidence.

fallacies.name: Appeal to law as proof of morality
fallacies.summary: The argument infers that an act is morally right or wrong solely from its legal status.
fallacies.body: The argument infers that an act is morally right or wrong solely from its legal status. Law and morality can diverge because laws may be unjust, permissive, or administratively motivated.

examples.text: Tax avoidance is moral because the statute permits it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Legality is treated as conclusive proof of moral permissibility or impermissibility.
doesNotCountWhen: Legal status is relevant to legal compliance and may be one moral consideration without settling morality alone.

fallacies.name: Appeal to loyalty
fallacies.summary: The argument treats loyalty to a group or person as a reason to accept the group's claim.
fallacies.body: The argument treats loyalty to a group or person as a reason to accept the group's claim. Loyalty can motivate solidarity but does not determine truth or correctness.

examples.text: You are loyal to our team, so you must agree that our defective product is safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Disagreement is framed as betrayal and loyalty substitutes for evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Loyalty is relevant to duties of allegiance when the conclusion concerns that duty rather than an unrelated factual claim.

fallacies.name: Appeal to motive
fallacies.summary: The argument rejects a claim because its speaker has a supposed motive for making it.
fallacies.body: The argument rejects a claim because its speaker has a supposed motive for making it. A motive may explain why someone asserts a proposition but does not show the proposition false.

examples.text: The inspector wants a promotion, so her finding that the building is unsafe is false.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The alleged motive is used as a refutation without addressing the inspection evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Motive evidence is relevant to credibility or bias assessment when it is combined with evidence bearing on reliability.

fallacies.name: Appeal to nature
fallacies.summary: The argument treats what is natural as automatically good, true, or preferable.
fallacies.body: The argument treats what is natural as automatically good, true, or preferable. Natural things can be harmful and artificial things can be beneficial; naturalness needs a specified normative link.

examples.text: This poison is natural, so consuming it is healthy.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion follows solely from a natural-versus-artificial description.
doesNotCountWhen: Naturalness is relevant when the stated goal specifically concerns ecological origin or when a supported mechanism connects it to the conclusion.

fallacies.name: Appeal to normality
fallacies.summary: The argument treats what is usual or statistically common as automatically right, safe, or true.
fallacies.body: The argument treats what is usual or statistically common as automatically right, safe, or true. Frequency does not entail value, correctness, or safety.

examples.text: Most adults sleep poorly, so sleeping poorly is healthy.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A claim's normality is offered as proof of its desirability or truth.
doesNotCountWhen: Normal prevalence is relevant to statistical description or risk estimates when not confused with normative approval.

fallacies.name: Appeal to novelty
fallacies.summary: The argument treats a newer claim, product, or method as superior merely because it is newer.
fallacies.body: The argument treats a newer claim, product, or method as superior merely because it is newer. Recency does not establish effectiveness, accuracy, or value.

examples.text: This new database must be more reliable than the old one because it was released this year.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion relies only on newness.
doesNotCountWhen: Novelty is relevant when new evidence, testing, or capabilities support the claimed improvement.

fallacies.name: Appeal to personal charm
fallacies.summary: The argument treats a speaker's likability or charisma as evidence for the speaker's claim.
fallacies.body: The argument treats a speaker's likability or charisma as evidence for the speaker's claim. Charm affects social response but does not establish factual or logical support.

examples.text: The consultant is warm and entertaining, so her forecast must be accurate.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Personal appeal is substituted for evidence relevant to the forecast.
doesNotCountWhen: A person's manner may appropriately affect judgments about rapport or communication, not truth by itself.

fallacies.name: Appeal to pity
fallacies.summary: The argument seeks acceptance of a conclusion by evoking sympathy instead of giving relevant reasons.
fallacies.body: The argument seeks acceptance of a conclusion by evoking sympathy instead of giving relevant reasons. Misfortune does not make a factual claim true or excuse an unrelated inference.

examples.text: The defendant should be found innocent because his children will suffer if he is convicted.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The audience's compassion is offered as the decisive support for innocence.
doesNotCountWhen: Pity is relevant to mercy or sentencing decisions when the issue is properly about consequences or mitigation.

fallacies.name: Appeal to popularity
fallacies.summary: The argument treats a proposition as true or right because many people favor it.
fallacies.body: The argument treats a proposition as true or right because many people favor it. Collective acceptance can be mistaken and does not entail truth or morality.

examples.text: Millions believe the supplement works, so it works.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion is supported only by the number of believers or supporters.
doesNotCountWhen: Popularity can be relevant evidence about preference, convention, or a source's prevalence, not conclusive proof.

fallacies.name: Appeal to possibility
fallacies.summary: The argument treats mere possibility as sufficient support for actuality or necessity.
fallacies.body: The argument treats mere possibility as sufficient support for actuality or necessity. A possible scenario may be remote, unsupported, or compatible with many conclusions.

examples.text: A hidden volcano could be under the city, so the evacuation is required today.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument moves from could be true to is true, must be acted on, or is likely without probability evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Possibility is a legitimate basis for contingency planning when likelihood, cost, and decision thresholds are considered.

fallacies.name: Appeal to poverty
fallacies.summary: The argument treats lack of money or low social status as evidence that a claim is false or true.
fallacies.body: The argument treats lack of money or low social status as evidence that a claim is false or true. Economic position does not determine competence, honesty, or factual accuracy.

examples.text: The researcher is poor, so her statistical result must be wrong.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The person's wealth or poverty is used as the decisive support for evaluating the proposition.
doesNotCountWhen: Resources can be relevant to access, incentives, or feasibility without proving the claim itself.

fallacies.name: Appeal to probability
fallacies.summary: The argument treats a statement as true merely because it is possible or probable, or treats probability as certainty.
fallacies.body: The argument treats a statement as true merely because it is possible or probable, or treats probability as certainty. Probability supports graded confidence, not an unconditional conclusion unless the decision rule warrants it.

examples.text: There is a 60 percent chance of rain, so it will rain.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The wording converts a probabilistic estimate into certainty or uses bare possibility as proof.
doesNotCountWhen: A probabilistic conclusion is sound when its probability estimate and assumptions support the stated degree of confidence.

fallacies.name: Appeal to ridicule
fallacies.summary: The argument mocks a claim or its proponent instead of answering the claim's reasons.
fallacies.body: The argument mocks a claim or its proponent instead of answering the claim's reasons. Ridicule may change attitudes but supplies no refutation.

examples.text: You believe the proposal will cut emissions; should we also ask a cartoon character to run the country?

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion is dismissed through derision rather than relevant counterargument.
doesNotCountWhen: Humor can expose an actual contradiction or communicate criticism when the underlying reasons are also given.

fallacies.name: Appeal to self-evident truth
fallacies.summary: The argument labels a disputed proposition self-evident instead of supporting it.
fallacies.body: The argument labels a disputed proposition self-evident instead of supporting it. Calling a claim obvious does not make its premises shared or its inference valid.

examples.text: It is self-evident that this economic policy will help everyone, so no analysis is necessary.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion is insulated from challenge by an unsupported assertion of obviousness.
doesNotCountWhen: A proposition may be self-evident within a defined formal system or after its meaning makes it analytically true.

fallacies.name: Appeal to spite
fallacies.summary: The argument supports a choice because it harms or frustrates an opponent.
fallacies.body: The argument supports a choice because it harms or frustrates an opponent. Harming an adversary does not establish that the chosen action is correct or beneficial.

examples.text: The merger will hurt our rival, so shareholders should approve it even though it loses money.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The opponent's loss is the main stated reason for the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: Spite may describe a motive or be relevant to a narrowly specified retaliatory policy, but it does not prove unrelated claims.

fallacies.name: Appeal to stupidity
fallacies.summary: The argument relies on an opponent's alleged stupidity to dismiss the opponent's claim.
fallacies.body: The argument relies on an opponent's alleged stupidity to dismiss the opponent's claim. Insulting intelligence neither identifies an error nor establishes the speaker's conclusion.

examples.text: Only an idiot would deny that the plan is safe, so the plan is safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response attacks alleged intelligence in place of analyzing the proposition.
doesNotCountWhen: Evidence that a person's reasoning is unreliable can be relevant when specifically demonstrated rather than asserted as an insult.

fallacies.name: Appeal to the moon
fallacies.summary: The argument rejects a proposal by predicting an implausible chain of exaggerated consequences without supporting links.
fallacies.body: The argument rejects a proposal by predicting an implausible chain of exaggerated consequences without supporting links. A remote or absurd outcome does not follow merely because a policy has some initial effect.

examples.text: If we allow one bicycle in the lobby, soon the moon will be filled with bicycles, so no bicycles are allowed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion depends on a dramatic slippery-slope chain whose intermediate steps lack evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A chain argument is legitimate when each causal step is supported and the endpoint is a realistic relevant risk.

fallacies.name: Appeal to tradition
fallacies.summary: The argument treats a practice or belief as correct because it has been followed for a long time.
fallacies.body: The argument treats a practice or belief as correct because it has been followed for a long time. Persistence can reflect inertia or past conditions rather than truth or moral validity.

examples.text: Our hiring test has always excluded part-time applicants, so the exclusion is fair.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Tradition is the sole or decisive warrant for continuing the practice.
doesNotCountWhen: Tradition can preserve tested knowledge or express an independently justified value when its merits are argued.

fallacies.name: Appeal to trust
fallacies.summary: The argument treats personal trust as sufficient proof of a claim.
fallacies.body: The argument treats personal trust as sufficient proof of a claim. Trust may rationally lower scrutiny in a relationship but does not itself entail truth.

examples.text: I trust the contractor, so his unsupported claim that the wiring is safe needs no inspection.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion rests on trust while relevant evidence is absent or ignored.
doesNotCountWhen: Trust is a defeasible reason to rely on testimony when the person's competence, honesty, and track record are relevant and proportionate.

fallacies.name: Appeal to wealth
fallacies.summary: The argument treats wealth as evidence that a person is correct, competent, or morally right.
fallacies.body: The argument treats wealth as evidence that a person is correct, competent, or morally right. Financial success can result from luck, exploitation, or unrelated skills and does not establish the claim.

examples.text: The billionaire says the investment is safe, so it is safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The person's money or status is the principal support for an unrelated conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: Wealth is relevant to facts about financial resources or experience when evidence connects it to the specific claim.

fallacies.name: Argument by assertion
fallacies.summary: The argument repeats a conclusion as though forceful assertion were evidence.
fallacies.body: The argument repeats a conclusion as though forceful assertion were evidence. A claim does not gain support merely by being stated confidently or without qualification.

examples.text: The policy works because it works; anyone who asks for data is avoiding reality.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: No independent premise supports the conclusion, and insistence is substituted for one.
doesNotCountWhen: A concise assertion is legitimate when it states a conclusion already supported by premises supplied elsewhere.

fallacies.name: Argument by fast talking
fallacies.summary: The argument uses speed and volume to prevent scrutiny of weak or irrelevant reasoning.
fallacies.body: The argument uses speed and volume to prevent scrutiny of weak or irrelevant reasoning. Delivery rate cannot repair invalid inferences or unsupported premises.

examples.text: The auditor asks for records, and the manager rapidly lists unrelated successes until declaring the accounts proven clean.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion depends on overwhelming the listener's processing time rather than answering objections.
doesNotCountWhen: Rapid speech is not fallacious when the content remains clear, relevant, and independently supported.

fallacies.name: Argument by gibberish
fallacies.summary: The argument uses meaningless or incoherent language as though it conveyed support.
fallacies.body: The argument uses meaningless or incoherent language as though it conveyed support. Words without determinate content cannot function as premises or establish a conclusion.

examples.text: The quantum synergy of fiscal resonance proves the policy's epistemic inevitability.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The supposed reasons cannot be interpreted into propositions with relevant truth conditions.
doesNotCountWhen: Technical language is not gibberish when its terms are defined and the statements have coherent inferential roles.

fallacies.name: Argument by pigheadedness
fallacies.summary: The argument treats refusal to revise a position as evidence that the position is correct.
fallacies.body: The argument treats refusal to revise a position as evidence that the position is correct. Stubbornness is a behavioral trait, not support for a proposition.

examples.text: I will never change my mind that the dam is safe, therefore the dam is safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker's persistence or refusal to consider counterevidence is offered as the warrant.
doesNotCountWhen: Firm commitment is rational when maintained because the evidence remains decisive and objections have been answered.

fallacies.name: Argument by repetition
fallacies.summary: The argument treats repeated assertion as increased evidence.
fallacies.body: The argument treats repeated assertion as increased evidence. Repetition can increase familiarity without increasing truth or evidential support.

examples.text: The vaccine causes infertility; it causes infertility; it causes infertility; therefore the claim is established.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The same unsupported proposition is repeated as the main or only support.
doesNotCountWhen: Repetition is legitimate for emphasis or memorization when independent reasons support the claim.

fallacies.name: Argument from fallacy
fallacies.summary: The argument concludes that a proposition is false because an argument for it contains a fallacy.
fallacies.body: The argument concludes that a proposition is false because an argument for it contains a fallacy. A bad argument fails to establish its conclusion but does not establish the conclusion's negation.

examples.text: The mayor's claim that the road is unsafe used an appeal to fear, so the road is safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The only reason for rejecting the conclusion is that one supporting argument was invalid.
doesNotCountWhen: Rejecting an unsupported argument while investigating the conclusion independently is not fallacious.

fallacies.name: Argument from ignorance
fallacies.summary: The argument infers that a proposition is true because it has not been disproved, or false because it has not been proved.
fallacies.body: The argument infers that a proposition is true because it has not been disproved, or false because it has not been proved. Absence of evidence is not generally evidence of absence unless the search would reliably detect the evidence.

examples.text: No one has proved that ghosts do not exist, so ghosts exist.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion relies only on a lack of proof or disproof without a justified burden of proof.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference can be valid when an exhaustive, reliable investigation should have found the relevant evidence or when a rule assigns the burden.

fallacies.name: Argument from inertia
fallacies.summary: Treating the fact that a practice continues as sufficient reason that it should continue.
fallacies.body: Treating the fact that a practice continues as sufficient reason that it should continue. This rhetoric label overlaps appeals to tradition and status quo reasoning. Continuity can affect transition costs, but its mere existence does not establish that the practice remains justified.

examples.text: We have always filed the reports twice, so we must keep doing it even though one filing now satisfies every requirement.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Continuation is justified solely by prior continuation, without addressing the relevant present reasons.
doesNotCountWhen: Stability, transition risk, or contractual commitments can supply independent reasons to retain a practice.

fallacies.name: Argument from mystery
fallacies.summary: Treating an unexplained event as positive evidence for a favored explanation without establishing the connection.
fallacies.body: Treating an unexplained event as positive evidence for a favored explanation without establishing the connection. A gap in current knowledge leaves a question open rather than assigning its answer. The preferred explanation must outperform alternatives through evidence, not merely occupy the gap.

examples.text: No one has identified the noise in the recording, so it proves a ghost was speaking.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Lack of an established explanation is the main support for one particular explanation.
doesNotCountWhen: An unfamiliar event can support a new hypothesis when independent discriminating evidence is supplied.

fallacies.name: Argument from necessity
fallacies.summary: Inferring that a claim is true because accepting it seems necessary for a desired purpose.
fallacies.body: Inferring that a claim is true because accepting it seems necessary for a desired purpose. Some rhetoric catalogs use the label for a version of appeal to consequences. Needing reassurance, coordination, or motivation does not establish the factual belief proposed to supply it.

examples.text: This forecast must be accurate because otherwise our financing plan cannot work.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A practical need for a belief is presented as evidence of that belief's truth.
doesNotCountWhen: An actual logical necessity established from premises is not this argumentative move.

fallacies.name: Argument from omniscience
fallacies.summary: Claiming certainty about others' unobserved thoughts or all possible cases without a basis for that knowledge.
fallacies.body: Claiming certainty about others' unobserved thoughts or all possible cases without a basis for that knowledge. The rhetoric label targets explanations that assume access the speaker has not established. An account of motives or universal behavior needs evidence appropriate to its scope.

examples.text: Every employee who supported the policy secretly wanted to harm the company, including those I have never met.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument relies on exhaustive or private knowledge without identifying evidence that could warrant it.
doesNotCountWhen: A limited claim about motives can be supported by documents, testimony, or other relevant evidence.

fallacies.name: Argument from personal incredulity
fallacies.summary: The argument rejects a claim because the speaker cannot imagine or understand how it could be true.
fallacies.body: The argument rejects a claim because the speaker cannot imagine or understand how it could be true. Personal difficulty understanding a mechanism does not show that the mechanism is impossible or false.

examples.text: I cannot imagine how evolution could produce this complexity, so evolution did not produce it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker's inability to conceive an explanation is the only stated reason for rejection.
doesNotCountWhen: Inability to understand can properly prompt a request for explanation or identify a genuine explanatory gap without proving falsity.

fallacies.name: Argument from silence
fallacies.summary: The argument infers a fact from the absence of a statement or record without showing that silence would be informative.
fallacies.body: The argument infers a fact from the absence of a statement or record without showing that silence would be informative. Silence may result from ignorance, irrelevance, loss, or a choice not to speak.

examples.text: The ancient chronicle does not mention the eclipse, so no eclipse occurred.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A missing mention is treated as evidence of nonoccurrence without a reliable expectation of reporting.
doesNotCountWhen: Silence is relevant when the source was present, informed, expected to report the fact, and the absence is unlikely under the fact's truth.

fallacies.name: Atomistic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Inferring a group-level relationship directly from an individual-level relationship without justification.
fallacies.body: Inferring a group-level relationship directly from an individual-level relationship without justification. Relationships between individuals need not match relationships between aggregate populations because composition and context can differ.

examples.text: Wealthier individuals are more likely to support Party A, so districts with higher average incomes must give Party A a larger vote share.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An association established at the individual level is asserted at an aggregate level without testing the cross-level inference.
doesNotCountWhen: Cross-level inference is justified when an appropriate model or independent aggregate evidence establishes the relationship.

fallacies.name: Avoiding the issue
fallacies.summary: The argument responds to a question or objection with an irrelevant point instead of addressing its substance.
fallacies.body: The argument responds to a question or objection with an irrelevant point instead of addressing its substance. An unrelated statement cannot establish the requested conclusion or answer the objection.

examples.text: Asked whether the report falsified the forecast, the analyst says the company has excellent branding.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response changes the subject while presenting the new point as though it resolved the original issue.
doesNotCountWhen: A response may redirect to a different issue when it explicitly explains that the original question is outside scope or when the new issue entails the answer.

fallacies.name: Base-rate fallacy
fallacies.summary: The argument neglects a relevant background frequency when interpreting specific evidence.
fallacies.body: The argument neglects a relevant background frequency when interpreting specific evidence. Specific evidence must be weighted against prior prevalence and the evidence's diagnostic reliability.

examples.text: A rare disease test is positive, so the patient almost certainly has the disease despite a very low base rate and imperfect specificity.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion uses a salient individual signal while ignoring a known population base rate.
doesNotCountWhen: Ignoring the base rate is not fallacious when the evidence is conditionally decisive or the base rate is irrelevant to the defined population.

fallacies.name: Begging the question
fallacies.summary: The argument assumes its conclusion, explicitly or implicitly, in the premises.
fallacies.body: The argument assumes its conclusion, explicitly or implicitly, in the premises. A premise that already presupposes the conclusion cannot provide independent support for it.

examples.text: This law is just because it is the right law, and it is the right law because it is just.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion is used as a premise without an independently supported reformulation.
doesNotCountWhen: A circular-looking phrase is acceptable when the premise and conclusion are genuinely different claims with independent support.

fallacies.name: Biased sample
fallacies.summary: The argument generalizes from a sample systematically unrepresentative of the population about which it concludes.
fallacies.body: The argument generalizes from a sample systematically unrepresentative of the population about which it concludes. Selection or measurement bias can make the observed proportion differ from the population proportion.

examples.text: An online poll of the party's subscribers shows that the entire city supports the candidate.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The sample excludes or overrepresents relevant groups in a way connected to the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A nonrepresentative sample can support conclusions about the sampled subgroup or about the population when weighting and design correct the bias.

fallacies.name: Big-lie technique
fallacies.summary: Treating repeated, emphatic assertion of a false or unsupported claim as if repetition supplied evidence.
fallacies.body: Treating repeated, emphatic assertion of a false or unsupported claim as if repetition supplied evidence. This is principally a propaganda tactic, and it becomes an argumentative defect when repetition stands in for support. Confidence, reach, and familiarity do not establish the underlying proposition.

examples.text: Every speech repeats that an election database was destroyed, even after the intact database is made available for inspection.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A claim's repetition or prominence is offered as a reason to accept it despite absent or contrary support.
doesNotCountWhen: Repeating a supported conclusion to communicate it is not itself a fallacy.

fallacies.name: Blind authority
fallacies.summary: The argument accepts a purported authority's statement without checking relevance, competence, evidence, or possible error.
fallacies.body: The argument accepts a purported authority's statement without checking relevance, competence, evidence, or possible error. Even legitimate authorities can be mistaken, misquoted, or outside their expertise.

examples.text: The professor said the bridge is safe, so I will not inspect the structural report.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Deference itself is treated as sufficient reason and all scrutiny is suspended.
doesNotCountWhen: Relying provisionally on a competent authority is reasonable when the domain, evidence, and source reliability are appropriate.

fallacies.name: Broken-window fallacy
fallacies.summary: The argument counts spending caused by destruction as a net economic benefit while ignoring the repair's opportunity cost.
fallacies.body: The argument counts spending caused by destruction as a net economic benefit while ignoring the repair's opportunity cost. Repair replaces resources that could have produced other benefits and does not create the lost asset's value.

examples.text: A vandal breaks a shop window, so the damage is good because the glazier earns money.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The analysis counts visible repair activity but omits what the shopkeeper would have bought without the damage.
doesNotCountWhen: Repair spending can create activity or employment, but the full comparison must include opportunity costs and the original loss.

fallacies.name: Bulverism
fallacies.summary: The argument explains why someone believes a claim by alleging a bias and then treats that alleged origin as a refutation.
fallacies.body: The argument explains why someone believes a claim by alleging a bias and then treats that alleged origin as a refutation. A belief's psychological or social cause does not determine whether the belief is true.

examples.text: You support free trade only because you are wealthy, so your argument for free trade is false.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response substitutes a speculation about the opponent's motives or class for evaluation of the argument.
doesNotCountWhen: Origins can be relevant to credibility or ideological bias while the proposition is still assessed on its evidence.

fallacies.name: Category mistake
fallacies.summary: The argument assigns a property or question to something that belongs to a different logical category.
fallacies.body: The argument assigns a property or question to something that belongs to a different logical category. Predicates and explanations applicable to one category may be meaningless or misplaced for another.

examples.text: After touring every college building, the visitor asks where the university itself is located.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The reasoning treats an abstract institution, property, relation, or object as though it were the wrong kind of entity.
doesNotCountWhen: A category assignment is legitimate when the predicate genuinely applies by a stated abstraction or institutional convention.

fallacies.name: Causal oversimplification
fallacies.summary: The argument attributes an outcome to one cause while ignoring other substantial causes or interactions.
fallacies.body: The argument attributes an outcome to one cause while ignoring other substantial causes or interactions. Complex outcomes often have multiple contributing conditions, so one factor may be insufficient.

examples.text: The harvest failed because of one late frost, although drought, pests, and soil depletion also caused losses.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A single cause is asserted as complete without ruling out relevant co-causes or mechanisms.
doesNotCountWhen: A single-cause explanation is sound when evidence shows the factor was sufficient or dominant for the defined outcome.

fallacies.name: Cherry-picking
fallacies.summary: The argument selects favorable evidence while ignoring relevant unfavorable evidence.
fallacies.body: The argument selects favorable evidence while ignoring relevant unfavorable evidence. Selective inclusion distorts the evidential balance and can create a misleading pattern.

examples.text: The supplement seller cites three customers who improved and omits the fifty who did not.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The evidence set is chosen by outcome or convenience in a way that supports the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: Selecting a relevant subset is legitimate when the selection rule is disclosed and justified for the stated question.

fallacies.name: Circular definition
fallacies.summary: The definition explains a term using the same term or a synonym that presupposes its meaning.
fallacies.body: The definition explains a term using the same term or a synonym that presupposes its meaning. A definition cannot clarify a concept if understanding it already requires understanding the defined word.

examples.text: A fair law is a law that treats people fairly.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The proposed definition provides no independent criterion for applying the term.
doesNotCountWhen: A recursive definition can be legitimate when it has a noncircular base case and a well-defined construction rule.

fallacies.name: Circular reasoning
fallacies.summary: The argument uses a conclusion or an equivalent proposition as support for that same conclusion.
fallacies.body: The argument uses a conclusion or an equivalent proposition as support for that same conclusion. The reasoning supplies no independent warrant, so a doubter has no reason to accept the premise.

examples.text: The witness is trustworthy because she gives reliable testimony, and her testimony is reliable because she is trustworthy.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The support for the conclusion depends on the conclusion or an equivalent claim.
doesNotCountWhen: A conclusion may rest on a premise that resembles it only superficially when the premise has independent evidence.

fallacies.name: Circumstantial ad hominem
fallacies.summary: The argument rejects a claim by pointing to the proponent's circumstances rather than the claim's reasons.
fallacies.body: The argument rejects a claim by pointing to the proponent's circumstances rather than the claim's reasons. A person's interests or situation can explain advocacy without making the advocated proposition false.

examples.text: The landlord says the building needs repair, but she owns the property, so the building is sound.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response treats an alleged conflict of interest as a refutation without examining the evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Circumstantial evidence may properly lower confidence or require corroboration when it bears on reliability, but it does not alone settle truth.

fallacies.name: Commutation of conditionals
fallacies.summary: Reversing a conditional without justification, inferring Q → P from P → Q.
fallacies.body: Reversing a conditional without justification, inferring Q → P from P → Q. A sufficient condition need not be necessary, so reversing the direction can change truth conditions.

examples.text: If the device is submerged, it stops working. Therefore, if it stops working, it must have been submerged.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A conditional is replaced by its converse without a premise establishing the reverse implication.
doesNotCountWhen: Reversal is justified when a biconditional or the converse is independently established.

fallacies.name: Complex question
fallacies.summary: The argument asks a question that presupposes a disputed claim so that any direct answer concedes it.
fallacies.body: The argument asks a question that presupposes a disputed claim so that any direct answer concedes it. A loaded presupposition must be separated and examined before the question is answered.

examples.text: Have you stopped falsifying your expense reports?

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The question embeds an unestablished assertion and treats yes or no as acceptance of it.
doesNotCountWhen: A question is not fallacious when its presupposition is established, explicitly conditional, or genuinely under examination.

fallacies.name: Composition fallacy
fallacies.summary: The argument infers that a whole has a property because each part has that property.
fallacies.body: The argument infers that a whole has a property because each part has that property. Properties of parts may not combine additively or survive organization and interaction.

examples.text: Every player on the team is an excellent solo athlete, so the team must be excellent.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The whole-level conclusion is supported only by the corresponding property of individual components.
doesNotCountWhen: Composition is valid when the property is known to transfer to the whole under the relevant structure.

fallacies.name: Conflicting conditions
fallacies.summary: The argument demands or relies on conditions that cannot all be satisfied simultaneously.
fallacies.body: The argument demands or relies on conditions that cannot all be satisfied simultaneously. An impossible conjunction cannot provide a workable basis for action or a consistent conclusion.

examples.text: The plan must spend nothing and also purchase the new equipment this quarter.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The stated requirements include mutually incompatible conditions under the same constraints.
doesNotCountWhen: Conditions are not fallacious when they are alternatives, sequenced, or made consistent by an unstated but available resource.

fallacies.name: Confusing explanation with excuse
fallacies.summary: The argument treats explaining why an act occurred as proving that the act was justified or excused.
fallacies.body: The argument treats explaining why an act occurred as proving that the act was justified or excused. A causal or psychological explanation does not by itself remove responsibility or wrongness.

examples.text: He stole because he was desperate, so stealing was morally permissible.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The explanation of the conduct is used as the conclusion that the conduct was acceptable.
doesNotCountWhen: An explanation can also support an excuse when a valid norm recognizes the stated condition as exculpatory.

fallacies.name: Confusing unexplained with unexplainable
fallacies.summary: The argument infers that a phenomenon cannot be explained because it has not yet been explained.
fallacies.body: The argument infers that a phenomenon cannot be explained because it has not yet been explained. Current ignorance is compatible with a future explanation and does not establish impossibility.

examples.text: No scientist has explained this dream, so the dream cannot have a natural cause.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion changes a present absence of explanation into a claim of principled inexplicability.
doesNotCountWhen: A phenomenon may be called unexplainable when a specified proof shows no explanation is possible within a defined system.

fallacies.name: Conjunction fallacy
fallacies.summary: The argument judges a conjunction of events more probable than one of its conjuncts.
fallacies.body: The argument judges a conjunction of events more probable than one of its conjuncts. A conjunction cannot be more probable than either component because it requires both to occur.

examples.text: Linda is more likely to be a bank teller and environmental activist than to be a bank teller.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The narrative representativeness of the combined description overrides the probability relation P(A and B) less than or equal to P(A).
doesNotCountWhen: A conjunction can be more specific or informative than a conjunct, but not more probable under the same probability model.

fallacies.name: Continuum fallacy
fallacies.summary: The argument denies a meaningful distinction because borderline cases form a gradual continuum.
fallacies.body: The argument denies a meaningful distinction because borderline cases form a gradual continuum. A continuous change can still contain useful thresholds or category differences for a defined purpose.

examples.text: There is no exact point at which a pile becomes a pile, so no collection can be called a pile.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The existence of vague intermediate cases is used to reject all categorical judgments.
doesNotCountWhen: A continuum warrants caution or graded classification when no principled threshold is available for the decision.

fallacies.name: Converse accident
fallacies.summary: The argument generalizes from a special case or exception to a broad rule.
fallacies.body: The argument generalizes from a special case or exception to a broad rule. An exceptional case may not represent ordinary cases and may involve unique conditions.

examples.text: A patient recovered without treatment, so medical treatment is unnecessary for everyone.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A narrow or exceptional instance is used to establish a universal or general conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A generalization is legitimate when the case is representative or supported by an adequate sample and causal analysis.

fallacies.name: Correlation implies causation
fallacies.summary: The argument infers that one correlated variable causes the other without establishing direction, mechanism, or confounding controls.
fallacies.body: The argument infers that one correlated variable causes the other without establishing direction, mechanism, or confounding controls. Correlation can result from reverse causation, common causes, coincidence, or selection effects.

examples.text: Ice-cream sales and drownings rise together, so buying ice cream causes drowning.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A statistical association is treated as sufficient proof of a causal relation.
doesNotCountWhen: Causal inference is justified when design, temporal order, controls, mechanism, or converging evidence support it.

fallacies.name: Defense attorney's fallacy
fallacies.summary: Dismissing incriminating evidence as worthless because many other people could also match it.
fallacies.body: Dismissing incriminating evidence as worthless because many other people could also match it. A possible match among other people does not make the evidence irrelevant; its weight depends on the prior information, likelihoods, and remaining evidence.

examples.text: A rare profile would match a thousand people in the country, so a lawyer claims the defendant's matching profile supplies no evidence at all despite independent evidence placing the defendant at the scene.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The existence of other possible matches is used to assign no evidential weight to a match while ignoring the relevant likelihood comparison and other evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Identifying alternative matches can correctly challenge a claim of unique identification; a match alone need not establish guilt beyond the required standard.

fallacies.name: Definist fallacy
fallacies.summary: The argument settles a substantive dispute by choosing a loaded definition that builds the desired conclusion into a term.
fallacies.body: The argument settles a substantive dispute by choosing a loaded definition that builds the desired conclusion into a term. A stipulative definition cannot by itself prove the substantive claim expressed with that term.

examples.text: Anyone who opposes this bill is a traitor, so opposing the bill is wrong.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A contested label is defined evaluatively and then used as if its definition established the judgment.
doesNotCountWhen: A stipulative definition is legitimate for setting terminology when its consequences are not confused with independent facts or values.

fallacies.name: Denying a conjunct
fallacies.summary: Inferring that one statement is true because the other is false and they cannot both be true.
fallacies.body: Inferring that one statement is true because the other is false and they cannot both be true. Not both P and Q permits both to be false; denying one does not establish the other.

examples.text: The office is not both open and staffed. It is not open, so it must be staffed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The form is ¬(P ∧ Q); ¬P; therefore Q, or its symmetric form.
doesNotCountWhen: Adding a justified premise that at least one of P and Q is true makes the inference valid.

fallacies.name: Denying the antecedent
fallacies.summary: The argument infers that the consequent is false from the falsity of a conditional's antecedent.
fallacies.body: The argument infers that the consequent is false from the falsity of a conditional's antecedent. A conditional does not say that the consequent has no other causes.

examples.text: If the switch is pressed, the lamp lights; the switch was not pressed, so the lamp is not lit.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The form is If A then B; not-A; therefore not-B, without a biconditional or exclusion of alternatives.
doesNotCountWhen: The conclusion follows when an additional justified premise establishes Q → P, including an explicit biconditional.

fallacies.name: Denying the correlative
fallacies.summary: The argument rejects a relation by denying one side's associated condition or status without addressing the relation's actual terms.
fallacies.body: The argument rejects a relation by denying one side's associated condition or status without addressing the relation's actual terms. Correlative concepts can be asymmetric or depend on a relation that is not removed by denying a label.

examples.text: There is no debtor here because the person has not been called a debtor, so no one is owed money.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A term or status is denied by renaming or denying its counterpart rather than testing the underlying relation.
doesNotCountWhen: Denying a correlative is legitimate when the relation's necessary condition is genuinely absent and the terms are used precisely.

fallacies.name: Disjunction fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assigning an inclusive disjunction a lower probability than one of its component events.
fallacies.body: Assigning an inclusive disjunction a lower probability than one of its component events. Every occurrence of A is an occurrence of A or B, so P(A ∨ B) cannot be less than P(A) under the same probability model.

examples.text: A forecaster assigns a twenty percent chance of snow but only a ten percent chance of rain or snow during the same period.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Comparable unconditional probabilities violate P(A ∨ B) ≥ P(A) or P(A ∨ B) ≥ P(B).
doesNotCountWhen: Probabilities referring to different conditions, periods, or an exclusive disjunction require a different comparison.

fallacies.name: Distinction without a difference
fallacies.summary: The argument introduces a verbal distinction while denying that the two cases differ in any relevant property.
fallacies.body: The argument introduces a verbal distinction while denying that the two cases differ in any relevant property. A distinction matters only if it changes the reasons, consequences, truth conditions, or applicable rule.

examples.text: The fee is not a tax because the invoice calls it a civic contribution, although both are compulsory charges funding the same service.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response changes terminology but identifies no relevant difference between the compared cases.
doesNotCountWhen: A distinction is legitimate when the categories differ in a property relevant to the conclusion or to the governing rule.

fallacies.name: Division fallacy
fallacies.summary: The properties of a whole are wrongly inferred for each part.
fallacies.body: The properties of a whole are wrongly inferred for each part. A group can have an aggregate property that none of its members has individually.

examples.text: The committee is slow to decide, so every committee member must be slow to decide.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument transfers a collective statistic or relation directly to each member without a linking premise.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is valid when the property is explicitly distributive or independently established for each part.

fallacies.name: Dog-whistle argument
fallacies.summary: Using coded associations to supply an unstated, unsupported reason for accepting a conclusion.
fallacies.body: Using coded associations to supply an unstated, unsupported reason for accepting a conclusion. Coded language is not inherently a logical fallacy. The argumentative defect occurs when a prejudicial association does the supporting work while remaining unavailable for explicit examination.

examples.text: Reject the candidate because you know what people from that neighborhood are like, without identifying any relevant conduct.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An intended audience is invited to infer an adverse conclusion through an unargued coded association.
doesNotCountWhen: Specialized shorthand that communicates a relevant, defensible premise is not inherently fallacious.

fallacies.name: Double standard
fallacies.summary: The same relevant conduct is judged by incompatible standards depending on who performs it.
