fallacies.body: The same relevant conduct is judged by incompatible standards depending on who performs it. Changing the rule with the person or faction makes the evaluation inconsistent rather than evidence-based.

examples.text: Our candidate may hide consulting income because privacy matters, but their candidate must disclose every private payment.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Comparable cases receive different approval thresholds with no relevant difference that explains the asymmetry.
doesNotCountWhen: Different standards are legitimate when the cases differ in a relevant feature such as role, risk, or evidence.

fallacies.name: Ecological fallacy
fallacies.summary: An individual is assigned a group-level relationship or average.
fallacies.body: An individual is assigned a group-level relationship or average. Aggregate correlations do not determine how variables relate within the aggregate.

examples.text: The district has high income and high literacy, so every resident there must be wealthy and literate.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A statistic about regions, schools, or populations is used as a prediction about each member.
doesNotCountWhen: A group statistic can legitimately describe a randomly selected member only with an appropriate probabilistic qualification.

fallacies.name: Equivocation
fallacies.summary: A key word changes meaning during the argument while appearing to remain the same.
fallacies.body: A key word changes meaning during the argument while appearing to remain the same. The conclusion depends on treating two senses as one fixed term.

examples.text: Only man is rational, and no woman is a man, so no woman is rational.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A repeated ambiguous term bridges premises whose truth depends on different definitions.
doesNotCountWhen: The argument is sound when the context clearly signals distinct senses or when the term is explicitly disambiguated.

fallacies.name: Etymological fallacy
fallacies.summary: A word is claimed to have its current meaning because of its historical origin.
fallacies.body: A word is claimed to have its current meaning because of its historical origin. Present usage is established by contemporary linguistic convention, not by a word's ancestry.

examples.text: The word nice once meant foolish, so calling a proposal nice cannot mean it is agreeable.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An etymology is offered as decisive evidence against a well-established modern sense.
doesNotCountWhen: Etymology legitimately explains history or helps infer an unfamiliar term's possible origin without dictating current meaning.

fallacies.name: Every-and-all fallacy
fallacies.summary: A universal claim is treated as though it guarantees an unrestricted conjunction of every related detail.
fallacies.body: A universal claim is treated as though it guarantees an unrestricted conjunction of every related detail. Universal quantifiers have a defined scope and do not add claims about unrelated attributes.

examples.text: Every employee signed the policy, so every employee signed every policy in the company.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument expands every or all beyond the noun, predicate, or scope actually quantified.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference counts when the original quantifier explicitly ranges over the broader collection.

fallacies.name: Exclusive premises
fallacies.summary: Two categorical premises that exclude a shared middle class are used to infer a conclusion.
fallacies.body: Two categorical premises that exclude a shared middle class are used to infer a conclusion. In a categorical syllogism, two negative premises do not connect the subject and predicate terms.

examples.text: No poets are engineers; no engineers are dancers; therefore no poets are dancers.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The premises are both negative categorical propositions and the conclusion purports to relate their end terms.
doesNotCountWhen: A conclusion may follow if an additional affirmative premise or another valid argument form supplies the missing connection.

fallacies.name: Existential fallacy
fallacies.summary: A universal categorical premise is treated as proving that its subject class has members.
fallacies.body: A universal categorical premise is treated as proving that its subject class has members. Universal statements can be true vacuously when the referenced class is empty.

examples.text: All unicorns are mammals; therefore some unicorns are mammals.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion asserts existence while the premises contain only universal claims with no existential import.
doesNotCountWhen: Existence is warranted when a premise explicitly says that a member exists or the logic adopts a stated existential assumption.

fallacies.name: Fact-to-fiction fallacy
fallacies.summary: A true fact is used as though it establishes an invented narrative built around that fact.
fallacies.body: A true fact is used as though it establishes an invented narrative built around that fact. Truth of one premise does not transfer to unsupported fictional details.

examples.text: The museum owns a Roman coin, so the curator must have found it in a secret tomb.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A verified observation is followed by a story whose intermediate events and motives are not evidenced.
doesNotCountWhen: A fictional elaboration is acceptable when it is clearly labeled as imagination rather than asserted as fact.

fallacies.name: Failure to elucidate
fallacies.summary: A claim is asserted or repeated without clarifying the terms, mechanism, or evidence needed to understand it.
fallacies.body: A claim is asserted or repeated without clarifying the terms, mechanism, or evidence needed to understand it. Without explication, listeners cannot determine what would make the claim true or false.

examples.text: The reform will restore freedom because it is a truly liberating reform.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument relies on slogans or opaque abstractions instead of defining its central claim or showing its support.
doesNotCountWhen: A concise statement is not defective when its terms are already clear in context and the needed reasons are supplied elsewhere.

fallacies.name: False analogy
fallacies.summary: A conclusion is drawn from a comparison despite a missing relevant similarity.
fallacies.body: A conclusion is drawn from a comparison despite a missing relevant similarity. Analogical support depends on similarities that make the conclusion likely, not on superficial resemblance.

examples.text: A smartphone is like a human brain because both process information, so replacing a phone battery should require brain surgery.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The compared cases share a surface feature but differ on the causal or structural feature relevant to the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: An analogy is legitimate when the shared features are relevant and the limits of the comparison are acknowledged.

fallacies.name: False attribution
fallacies.summary: A statement, action, or work is incorrectly assigned to a person or source.
fallacies.body: A statement, action, or work is incorrectly assigned to a person or source. Evidence about the alleged source cannot support a claim when the source did not produce it.

examples.text: The mayor said the bridge was unsafe, but the quotation came from an anonymous engineer's report.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument relies on a quotation, discovery, or responsibility whose authorship is unsupported or contradicted.
doesNotCountWhen: Attribution is reasonable when provenance is documented or presented explicitly as uncertain.

fallacies.name: False balance
fallacies.summary: Opposing positions are presented as equally credible despite a substantial difference in evidence.
fallacies.body: Opposing positions are presented as equally credible despite a substantial difference in evidence. Fair reporting does not require equal weight for claims with unequal support.

examples.text: One hundred clinical studies find a treatment effective and one unreplicated blog post rejects it, so both sides are equally established.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The presentation gives symmetric time, authority, or confidence to claims with markedly asymmetric evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Balance is appropriate when the evidence is genuinely contested or when the purpose is to represent public viewpoints rather than truth-weight them.

fallacies.name: False cause
fallacies.summary: A causal connection is asserted without adequate evidence that one event produced the other.
fallacies.body: A causal connection is asserted without adequate evidence that one event produced the other. Temporal order or correlation alone does not establish the required causal mechanism and controls.

examples.text: The town installed new benches and crime fell, so the benches caused the decline.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion uses coincidence, sequence, or association as its only causal support.
doesNotCountWhen: The causal claim is warranted when controlled evidence, a credible mechanism, or converging observations support it.

fallacies.name: False dilemma
fallacies.summary: A choice is presented as limited to two alternatives when relevant options remain.
fallacies.body: A choice is presented as limited to two alternatives when relevant options remain. Excluding viable alternatives can make a forced conclusion appear necessary when it is not.

examples.text: Either we ban all cars or we accept deadly pollution forever.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument uses either-or language while omitting a plausible third policy, intermediate degree, or combined option.
doesNotCountWhen: A dilemma is valid when the alternatives are exhaustive for the stated context and genuinely incompatible.

fallacies.name: False effect
fallacies.summary: An alleged effect is treated as evidence for a cause or condition without establishing that the effect follows from it.
fallacies.body: An alleged effect is treated as evidence for a cause or condition without establishing that the effect follows from it. An outcome may have many causes or may not reliably indicate the proposed explanation.

examples.text: The alarm did not sound, so the building must be safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument treats a non-diagnostic outcome as a guaranteed consequence or indicator of the claimed state.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is legitimate when the effect is known to be necessary or sufficiently reliable under the stated conditions.

fallacies.name: False equivalence
fallacies.summary: Two subjects are declared equivalent despite a relevant difference in magnitude, kind, evidence, or responsibility.
fallacies.body: Two subjects are declared equivalent despite a relevant difference in magnitude, kind, evidence, or responsibility. Shared labels or one common feature do not erase differences that matter to the conclusion.

examples.text: A rude tweet and a violent assault are the same because both hurt someone's feelings.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The comparison uses an abstract similarity to dismiss a material asymmetry.
doesNotCountWhen: Equivalence is sound when the compared respects and relevant standards are explicitly the same.

fallacies.name: False precision
fallacies.summary: An estimate is expressed with unjustified numerical exactness.
fallacies.body: An estimate is expressed with unjustified numerical exactness. Extra digits imply measurement resolution and certainty that the method does not provide.

examples.text: The survey predicts exactly 63,217 future voters from a rough sample of 800 respondents.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A number has more significant figures or narrower uncertainty than the data and method support.
doesNotCountWhen: Precision is appropriate when the measurement process, sample, and uncertainty justify the stated resolution.

fallacies.name: False trilemma
fallacies.summary: Three options are presented as exhaustive when other possibilities exist.
fallacies.body: Three options are presented as exhaustive when other possibilities exist. Adding a third horn does not make a classification complete.

examples.text: You can be loyal, disloyal, or indifferent, so no one can be both loyal and critical.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument claims only three paths while omitting mixed, intermediate, or independent alternatives.
doesNotCountWhen: A trilemma is valid when the three options are explicitly exhaustive and mutually exclusive in context.

fallacies.name: Fantasy projection
fallacies.summary: A desired imagined outcome is treated as a prediction about reality.
fallacies.body: A desired imagined outcome is treated as a prediction about reality. Wishful imagery supplies no evidence that the imagined future will occur.

examples.text: I can picture our startup serving millions, so investors will certainly fund it next month.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument moves from vivid desire or visualization to confidence about an external event.
doesNotCountWhen: Planning can use imagined scenarios when they are marked as possibilities and tested against evidence.

fallacies.name: Far-fetched hypothesis
fallacies.summary: An unusually implausible explanation is accepted without evidence proportional to its extraordinary assumptions.
fallacies.body: An unusually implausible explanation is accepted without evidence proportional to its extraordinary assumptions. A hypothesis requiring many unsupported conditions has a low prior plausibility and needs strong support.

examples.text: The missing files were probably stolen by a spy using a trained pigeon because that could happen.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The explanation introduces elaborate rare mechanisms merely to preserve a preferred conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A far-fetched hypothesis is rational when independent evidence specifically predicts its unusual features.

fallacies.name: Faulty comparison
fallacies.summary: A conclusion about one case is drawn by comparing it with a case that differs in relevant respects.
fallacies.body: A conclusion about one case is drawn by comparing it with a case that differs in relevant respects. Comparability requires matching the variables that bear on the conclusion.

examples.text: This medicine worked for my cousin, so it will work for a newborn with a different disease.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The cases share an outcome or label but differ in population, conditions, or mechanism relevant to the inference.
doesNotCountWhen: Comparison is sound when those relevant differences are controlled or shown not to matter.

fallacies.name: Faulty inductive conversion
fallacies.summary: A probabilistic or particular claim is reversed so that its converse is treated as equally supported.
fallacies.body: A probabilistic or particular claim is reversed so that its converse is treated as equally supported. Evidence that A often accompanies B does not show that B usually indicates A.

examples.text: Most professional musicians practice daily, so anyone who practices daily is probably a professional musician.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument switches the direction of an inductive relation without new base-rate or causal evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Conversion is justified when symmetry is established by data or by a valid definition.

fallacies.name: Feedback fallacy
fallacies.summary: A result produced by a feedback loop is treated as though it were independent evidence for the original claim.
fallacies.body: A result produced by a feedback loop is treated as though it were independent evidence for the original claim. Self-reinforcing measurements can reflect the process that generated them rather than an external fact.

examples.text: The algorithm labels a neighborhood risky, police patrol it more, arrests rise, and the arrests prove the algorithm was right.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The evidence is an output that the original classification or intervention helped create.
doesNotCountWhen: Feedback evidence is useful when the loop is modeled, controlled, or independently validated.

fallacies.name: Fixed-pie fallacy
fallacies.summary: A benefit to one party is assumed necessarily to reduce another party's share by the same amount.
fallacies.body: A benefit to one party is assumed necessarily to reduce another party's share by the same amount. Resources, value, and opportunities can expand, contract, or be redistributed in ways that are not zero-sum.

examples.text: If another country exports more software to us, our workers must have lost exactly that much wealth.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument assumes a fixed total without showing a conservation constraint.
doesNotCountWhen: A fixed-pie model is appropriate when the relevant resource is explicitly fixed in quantity and scope.

fallacies.name: Four-term fallacy
fallacies.summary: A categorical syllogism contains four effective terms because a term shifts meaning or is introduced implicitly.
fallacies.body: A categorical syllogism contains four effective terms because a term shifts meaning or is introduced implicitly. A syllogism requires exactly three stable terms for the middle term to connect the others.

examples.text: All bats are animals, and all animals have rights, so all baseball bats have rights.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A word appears in two premises but denotes different classes, creating four terms rather than three.
doesNotCountWhen: There is no four-term fallacy when the repeated term keeps one unambiguous meaning throughout.

fallacies.name: Furtive fallacy
fallacies.summary: A failure to observe an event is treated as evidence that the event did not occur because it was supposedly hidden.
fallacies.body: A failure to observe an event is treated as evidence that the event did not occur because it was supposedly hidden. Non-observation cannot refute a claim when the event would be difficult or impossible to detect.

examples.text: No one saw the theft, so no theft occurred.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument treats absence of detection as disproof without showing that the event would have been noticed.
doesNotCountWhen: Non-observation is probative when the observation process had high coverage and the event would be conspicuous.

fallacies.name: Gadarene-swine fallacy
fallacies.summary: An argument is accepted or rejected because its consequences seem emotionally or socially extreme rather than because its premises support it.
fallacies.body: An argument is accepted or rejected because its consequences seem emotionally or socially extreme rather than because its premises support it. A frightening consequence does not determine whether the inference is valid or whether the premise is true.

examples.text: If we allow one late assignment, soon every student will demand a degree without attending class, so the exception is impossible.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The reasoning relies on an alarmist cascade from a small premise instead of establishing each causal step.
doesNotCountWhen: A cascade is legitimate when each step is supported and the alleged consequence follows under stated conditions.

fallacies.name: Galileo fallacy
fallacies.summary: A person compares opposition to their claim with historical persecution of a great thinker to imply that opposition proves correctness.
fallacies.body: A person compares opposition to their claim with historical persecution of a great thinker to imply that opposition proves correctness. Being resisted is compatible with being right or wrong and supplies no content-specific evidence.

examples.text: Scientists reject my perpetual-motion machine, just as authorities rejected Galileo, so my machine must work.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Dismissal or criticism is framed as evidence that the speaker is a persecuted truth-teller.
doesNotCountWhen: Historical analogy can be relevant when it identifies a documented pattern of institutional error, not merely dissent.

fallacies.name: Gambler's fallacy
fallacies.summary: After independent random outcomes, a less frequent outcome is expected because it is due.
fallacies.body: After independent random outcomes, a less frequent outcome is expected because it is due. Independent trials do not remember earlier results, so their probabilities remain unchanged.

examples.text: A fair coin has landed heads five times, so tails is now more likely on the next toss.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument changes the next-trial probability solely because of the preceding sequence.
doesNotCountWhen: A prediction is valid when trials are dependent or when a finite sampling rule creates a genuine remaining quota.

fallacies.name: Genetic fallacy
fallacies.summary: A claim is accepted or rejected solely because of its origin rather than its present reasons or evidence.
fallacies.body: A claim is accepted or rejected solely because of its origin rather than its present reasons or evidence. A source's history can be relevant to credibility but does not determine the claim's truth.

examples.text: The climate report was funded by an oil company, so every temperature measurement in it is false.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument substitutes provenance for evaluation of the proposition's supporting evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Origin is relevant when it directly bears on reliability, conflict of interest, or the causal history of the claim.

fallacies.name: Gish gallop
fallacies.summary: A speaker overwhelms an opponent with many weak or unrelated claims faster than they can be answered.
fallacies.body: A speaker overwhelms an opponent with many weak or unrelated claims faster than they can be answered. The volume of objections does not increase their individual merit and exploits limited response time.

examples.text: The debate opponent lists thirty alleged flaws in the study, each in one sentence, and declares victory when none is answered immediately.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A large rapid bundle of claims is used so that rebuttal cannot track, prioritize, and answer them individually.
doesNotCountWhen: A long list is legitimate when the claims are relevant, supported, and presented with a fair opportunity to address them.

fallacies.name: Guilt by association
fallacies.summary: A person or claim is condemned because of an alleged association with a disapproved person or group.
fallacies.body: A person or claim is condemned because of an alleged association with a disapproved person or group. Association alone does not show agreement, responsibility, or falsity.

examples.text: Lena attended the same conference as a cult leader, so Lena's research must be cult propaganda.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument supplies a disliked associate as the main reason to reject the target.
doesNotCountWhen: Association is relevant when evidence shows collaboration, shared commitments, or responsibility for the disputed conduct.

fallacies.name: Hasty generalization
fallacies.summary: A broad population conclusion is drawn from too few or unrepresentative cases.
fallacies.body: A broad population conclusion is drawn from too few or unrepresentative cases. A small biased sample may not reflect the population's actual distribution.

examples.text: Two taxis overcharged me, so every taxi driver in the city is dishonest.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion quantifies or stereotypes a population from an inadequate sample.
doesNotCountWhen: Generalization is reasonable when the sample is sufficiently large, representative, and measured for the claim.

fallacies.name: Having your cake
fallacies.summary: A position claims the benefits of two incompatible conditions while denying the cost or incompatibility.
fallacies.body: A position claims the benefits of two incompatible conditions while denying the cost or incompatibility. Mutually exclusive requirements cannot both be satisfied merely by asserting them.

examples.text: The company demands complete employee availability and guarantees that no employee will ever work extra hours.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument promises outcomes that jointly require conflicting constraints without explaining a tradeoff or mechanism.
doesNotCountWhen: Both outcomes can be retained when they are genuinely compatible under specified resources or conditions.

fallacies.name: Hedging
fallacies.summary: A claim is made vague or qualified enough to evade assessment while still suggesting a stronger conclusion.
fallacies.body: A claim is made vague or qualified enough to evade assessment while still suggesting a stronger conclusion. Strategic ambiguity prevents the audience from knowing what evidence would confirm or refute the claim.

examples.text: The supplement may perhaps support wellness in some sense, so critics cannot say it does nothing.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker shifts among vague qualifiers whenever a precise prediction or responsibility is requested.
doesNotCountWhen: Careful uncertainty is legitimate when the degree of confidence and the scope of the claim are made explicit.

fallacies.name: Heroes-all fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating membership in an admired group as proof that every member's conduct or claim deserves approval.
fallacies.body: Treating membership in an admired group as proof that every member's conduct or claim deserves approval. This is a nonstandard rhetoric label for blanket endorsement by association. Respect for a role does not eliminate the need to assess particular acts or propositions.

examples.text: Every member of this celebrated rescue team must be honest, so no allegation against any member needs investigation.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: General admiration for a group is used to exempt each member from relevant scrutiny.
doesNotCountWhen: Recognizing a group's achievements does not imply that all its members are beyond criticism.

fallacies.name: Historian's fallacy
fallacies.summary: Past actors are judged as though they had the information and options available only after later events.
fallacies.body: Past actors are judged as though they had the information and options available only after later events. Retrospective knowledge changes how alternatives appear and can distort assessment of the original decision.

examples.text: The general was obviously irrational not to evacuate before the ambush, because we now know exactly where it occurred.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The evaluation uses subsequent outcomes or discoveries as if they were known at the historical decision point.
doesNotCountWhen: Retrospective criticism is fair when it uses information actually available to the actors or clearly separates outcome from decision quality.

fallacies.name: Hollow man
fallacies.summary: A position is attacked after its substantive content is removed or replaced with a weaker slogan.
fallacies.body: A position is attacked after its substantive content is removed or replaced with a weaker slogan. Refuting a caricature does not refute the original position.

examples.text: The proposal funds targeted addiction treatment, but the reply says its supporters want unlimited government handouts.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The opponent's view is simplified into an extreme claim that its proponents do not defend.
doesNotCountWhen: Simplification is legitimate when it preserves the position's essential commitments and is accepted by its advocate.

fallacies.name: Homunculus fallacy
fallacies.summary: An explanation invokes a smaller agent with the same unexplained ability as the thing being explained.
fallacies.body: An explanation invokes a smaller agent with the same unexplained ability as the thing being explained. Relocating a problem inside a hypothetical inner person does not explain its mechanism.

examples.text: We recognize faces because a little face-recognizer in the brain recognizes them.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The explanation introduces an inner observer or controller without explaining how that entity performs the required task.
doesNotCountWhen: A subsystem is not a homunculus when its distinct operations are independently specified and mechanistically explained.

fallacies.name: Honor by association
fallacies.summary: A claim is treated as credible or true because a respected person or group is associated with it.
fallacies.body: A claim is treated as credible or true because a respected person or group is associated with it. Prestige does not substitute for evidence relevant to the proposition.

examples.text: A Nobel laureate endorsed this investment, so the investment cannot lose money.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument uses admiration for an associate as its principal support for an unrelated claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Expert association is relevant when the person has demonstrated expertise on the precise subject and gives reasons or evidence.

fallacies.name: Hot-hand fallacy
fallacies.summary: A run of successful independent attempts is treated as evidence that the next attempt is more likely to succeed.
fallacies.body: A run of successful independent attempts is treated as evidence that the next attempt is more likely to succeed. Past independent outcomes do not by themselves alter the next attempt's probability.

examples.text: A roulette bettor wins four independent spins and concludes the next identical bet now has a higher chance of winning because of the streak.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion raises the next-trial probability solely from a recent streak without evidence of changing skill or conditions.
doesNotCountWhen: A hot-hand inference is justified when data show serial dependence or a real temporary change in performance.

fallacies.name: Hypnotic bait-and-switch
fallacies.summary: A compelling but irrelevant cue attracts assent before the argument quietly substitutes a different claim.
fallacies.body: A compelling but irrelevant cue attracts assent before the argument quietly substitutes a different claim. Agreement elicited by attention, rhythm, or suggestion does not transfer to an unexamined proposition.

examples.text: The speaker uses soothing repetition to get agreement that the plan is compassionate, then treats that assent as agreement that it is affordable.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The persuasive trigger concerns one attitude while the conclusion relies on a different unstated proposition.
doesNotCountWhen: Rhetorical framing is legitimate when the audience can inspect the same claim that the framing supports.

fallacies.name: Identity fallacy
fallacies.summary: A person's identity or group membership is treated as sufficient evidence for or against the truth of a proposition.
fallacies.body: A person's identity or group membership is treated as sufficient evidence for or against the truth of a proposition. Identity may shape perspective but does not logically settle an empirical or conceptual claim.

examples.text: She is an immigrant, so her account of the border policy must be correct.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument substitutes demographic status for reasons addressing the claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Identity is relevant when the proposition concerns lived experience or when it supplies contextual evidence, not automatic correctness.

fallacies.name: If-by-whiskey
fallacies.summary: Ambiguous wording lets a speaker appear to support or oppose a policy while appealing differently to different audiences.
fallacies.body: Ambiguous wording lets a speaker appear to support or oppose a policy while appealing differently to different audiences. A conclusion cannot be evaluated until the operative meaning and commitment are made stable.

examples.text: I support responsible regulation of whiskey, meaning either sensible safeguards or whatever restrictions opponents deserve.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker uses a value-laden qualifier whose interpretation changes with the audience's preference.
doesNotCountWhen: Rhetorical ambiguity is acceptable in poetry or diplomacy when no precise factual commitment is being claimed.

fallacies.name: Ignoratio elenchi
fallacies.summary: The premises support a conclusion different from the one that the argument purports to establish.
fallacies.body: The premises support a conclusion different from the one that the argument purports to establish. Relevance to a nearby issue does not prove the target proposition.

examples.text: The defendant deserves kindness because prison is unpleasant, so he is legally innocent.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The reasons address punishment, character, or emotion while the conclusion concerns guilt or another unproved issue.
doesNotCountWhen: The argument is relevant when its actual conclusion is the proposition under evaluation or a stated subclaim needed for it.

fallacies.name: Ignoring a common cause
fallacies.summary: A correlation between two effects is treated as direct causation while a shared cause is neglected.
fallacies.body: A correlation between two effects is treated as direct causation while a shared cause is neglected. A third variable can generate both observations without either causing the other.

examples.text: Ice-cream sales and drownings rise together, so buying ice cream causes drowning.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument infers a direct link from association while omitting a plausible common driver such as hot weather.
doesNotCountWhen: Direct causation remains supported when common causes are controlled or the mechanism distinguishes it.

fallacies.name: Illicit contraposition
fallacies.summary: A categorical proposition is contraposed in a form whose distribution or quantity makes the inference invalid.
fallacies.body: A categorical proposition is contraposed in a form whose distribution or quantity makes the inference invalid. Contraposition is valid only for certain universal affirmative or particular negative forms under classical rules.

examples.text: Some poets are musicians, so some non-musicians are non-poets.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument replaces subject and predicate with their complements without checking the proposition's valid contraposition conditions.
doesNotCountWhen: Contraposition is legitimate for forms such as all A are B implying all non-B are non-A.

fallacies.name: Illicit conversion
fallacies.summary: The subject and predicate of a categorical proposition are simply exchanged even though the converse is not entailed.
fallacies.body: The subject and predicate of a categorical proposition are simply exchanged even though the converse is not entailed. Conversion preserves truth only for forms whose term distribution permits it.

examples.text: All cats are mammals, so all mammals are cats.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion reverses an asymmetric inclusion or relation without an added premise.
doesNotCountWhen: Conversion is valid for forms such as no A are B or some A are B when their terms remain properly distributed.

fallacies.name: Illicit major
fallacies.summary: A categorical syllogism distributes the major term in the conclusion without distributing it in the major premise.
fallacies.body: A categorical syllogism distributes the major term in the conclusion without distributing it in the major premise. The conclusion makes a claim about the whole major class that the premise did not license.

examples.text: All dogs are mammals; no cats are dogs; therefore no cats are mammals.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: In a standard-form syllogism, the major term is distributed in the conclusion but not in its premise.
doesNotCountWhen: The syllogism is valid when the major term is distributed in the major premise or the conclusion has a different valid form.

fallacies.name: Illicit minor
fallacies.summary: A categorical syllogism distributes the minor term in the conclusion without distributing it in the minor premise.
fallacies.body: A categorical syllogism distributes the minor term in the conclusion without distributing it in the minor premise. The conclusion makes a claim about the whole minor class unsupported by the premise.

examples.text: All cats are mammals; all cats are pets; therefore all pets are mammals.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: In a standard-form syllogism, the minor term is distributed in the conclusion but not in its premise.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is valid when the minor term is distributed in its premise or another valid syllogistic structure applies.

fallacies.name: Illicit substitution of identicals
fallacies.summary: Identical references are substituted inside a context where the substitution changes truth because the context is intensional.
fallacies.body: Identical references are substituted inside a context where the substitution changes truth because the context is intensional. Co-reference preserves truth in extensional contexts but not in belief, necessity, quotation, or other opaque contexts.

examples.text: The morning star is the evening star, and Ana believes the morning star is bright, so Ana believes the evening star is bright.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument replaces one co-referring name within a belief or similar opaque report without evidence that the subject recognizes the identity.
doesNotCountWhen: Substitution is valid in extensional contexts or when the relevant agent knows and accepts the identity.

fallacies.name: Incomplete comparison
fallacies.summary: A comparative claim omits the reference class or dimension needed to determine what is being compared.
fallacies.body: A comparative claim omits the reference class or dimension needed to determine what is being compared. Without the comparison standard, the claim can sound informative while making no definite assertion.

examples.text: Our new battery is better, so consumers should buy it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument uses better, safer, or faster without specifying than what, in which respect, or under what conditions.
doesNotCountWhen: A comparison is complete when its baseline, metric, and relevant conditions are stated or unambiguous.

fallacies.name: Inconsistency
fallacies.summary: The argument or position asserts propositions that cannot all be true under the same interpretation.
fallacies.body: The argument or position asserts propositions that cannot all be true under the same interpretation. Contradictory commitments prevent a stable conclusion and may allow arbitrary claims by explosion in classical logic.

examples.text: This rule applies to everyone, and it never applies to employees in my department.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The same subject, predicate, and conditions are both affirmed and denied without a resolving distinction.
doesNotCountWhen: Apparent inconsistency is harmless when the statements concern different times, senses, contexts, or explicitly qualified exceptions.

fallacies.name: Inflation of conflict
fallacies.summary: A disagreement about one issue is expanded into a claim of total opposition or irreconcilable conflict.
fallacies.body: A disagreement about one issue is expanded into a claim of total opposition or irreconcilable conflict. Partial disagreement can coexist with shared premises, goals, or many compatible conclusions.

examples.text: The parties disagree about the tax rate, so they have nothing in common politically.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A narrow disputed proposition is used to characterize the entire relationship or worldview as opposed.
doesNotCountWhen: Conflict may be broad when independent evidence shows disagreement across the relevant range of issues.

fallacies.name: Insignificant cause
fallacies.summary: A minor contributing condition is presented as the decisive or sufficient cause of a substantial outcome.
fallacies.body: A minor contributing condition is presented as the decisive or sufficient cause of a substantial outcome. A cause can be real yet too small to explain the observed magnitude or importance.

examples.text: A single typo caused the company's year-long collapse despite insolvency and lost contracts.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument elevates a small factor while ignoring larger necessary or enabling causes.
doesNotCountWhen: A small cause is an adequate explanation when the outcome is highly sensitive to it and alternatives are excluded.

fallacies.name: Inverse-probability fallacy
fallacies.summary: The probability of evidence given a hypothesis is confused with the probability of the hypothesis given the evidence.
fallacies.body: The probability of evidence given a hypothesis is confused with the probability of the hypothesis given the evidence. Bayes' rule requires prior probabilities and competing likelihoods, not a simple inversion.

examples.text: The test is 99 percent accurate if a disease is present, so a positive result means there is a 99 percent chance the patient has it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument reverses P(evidence|hypothesis) into P(hypothesis|evidence) without base rates or alternatives.
doesNotCountWhen: The reversed probability is justified only when the relevant priors and likelihoods happen to make the values equal.

fallacies.name: Irrelevant reason
fallacies.summary: A premise is offered as a reason for a conclusion even though it does not bear on that conclusion.
fallacies.body: A premise is offered as a reason for a conclusion even though it does not bear on that conclusion. A true or emotionally compelling statement can still fail to support the issue at hand.

examples.text: The park proposal is good because the speaker has a pleasant voice.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The stated reason concerns a topic, trait, or fact with no logical connection to the target claim.
doesNotCountWhen: A reason is relevant when changing its truth would materially alter the probability or justification of the conclusion.

fallacies.name: Is–ought fallacy
fallacies.summary: A normative conclusion is inferred from descriptive facts without a value premise linking facts to obligations.
fallacies.body: A normative conclusion is inferred from descriptive facts without a value premise linking facts to obligations. Descriptions alone do not specify what should be valued or required.

examples.text: People often lie to protect themselves, so lying is morally permissible.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument moves from what is, happens, or is natural directly to what ought to be done.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is valid when an explicit normative principle supplies the missing bridge.

fallacies.name: Jumping to conclusions
fallacies.summary: A definite conclusion is adopted before enough evidence or alternative explanations are considered.
fallacies.body: A definite conclusion is adopted before enough evidence or alternative explanations are considered. Premature closure makes uncertainty look resolved and can select an arbitrary explanation.

examples.text: The manager saw a late employee carrying a box and concluded that the employee was stealing.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The claim is stated with confidence despite sparse observations and untested competing hypotheses.
doesNotCountWhen: A quick conclusion is reasonable when the evidence is decisive or the cost of delay makes a calibrated provisional decision necessary.

fallacies.name: Just-because fallacy
fallacies.summary: A proposition is treated as justified merely because it is asserted as a reason or because no further explanation is supplied.
fallacies.body: A proposition is treated as justified merely because it is asserted as a reason or because no further explanation is supplied. Repeating a claim does not provide independent support for it.

examples.text: The rule is fair just because it is fair, so no evidence about its effects is needed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument uses the conclusion, a restatement, or an unexplained assertion as its only support.
doesNotCountWhen: A basic premise may be accepted without further argument when it is stipulated or independently established in the context.

fallacies.name: Just-in-case fallacy
fallacies.summary: An action is justified solely by a remote possibility, without weighing probability, cost, or benefit.
fallacies.body: An action is justified solely by a remote possibility, without weighing probability, cost, or benefit. Precaution must be proportionate to the risk and the available alternatives.

examples.text: We should ban all home cooking just in case one meal causes an undetected illness.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument treats any imaginable hazard as sufficient for a burdensome response.
doesNotCountWhen: Precaution is rational when the potential harm is serious and the intervention is proportionate to credible risk.

fallacies.name: Kettle logic
fallacies.summary: Several mutually inconsistent defenses are offered so that one may survive even if another fails.
fallacies.body: Several mutually inconsistent defenses are offered so that one may survive even if another fails. Contradictory explanations cannot jointly support the same conclusion without distinguishing conditions.

examples.text: The defendant says the document was never written, was written by someone else, and was written by him under coercion.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker shifts among incompatible accounts instead of resolving which account is asserted.
doesNotCountWhen: Alternative defenses are legitimate when presented explicitly as mutually exclusive possibilities supported by separate evidence.

fallacies.name: Least-plausible hypothesis
fallacies.summary: Among competing explanations, the least credible is selected without evidence that outweighs its lower plausibility.
fallacies.body: Among competing explanations, the least credible is selected without evidence that outweighs its lower plausibility. A hypothesis with implausible assumptions needs stronger likelihood evidence than ordinary alternatives.

examples.text: The lights went out because aliens disabled the grid, although a documented transformer failure occurred nearby.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument chooses an extraordinary explanation while ignoring simpler, better-supported causes.
doesNotCountWhen: The unusual hypothesis is warranted when distinctive evidence makes it predict the observations better than rivals.

fallacies.name: Logic chopping
fallacies.summary: A formal distinction or technical objection is used to dismiss relevant evidence without addressing its substance.
fallacies.body: A formal distinction or technical objection is used to dismiss relevant evidence without addressing its substance. Correct precision about terms cannot by itself defeat a claim supported on the merits.

examples.text: The study says participants improved, but because it did not use the word improved in the title, its result is irrelevant.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument fixates on wording, labels, or minor logical form while ignoring the actual evidential issue.
doesNotCountWhen: Technical analysis is legitimate when the disputed distinction changes the truth or validity of the claim.

fallacies.name: Ludic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Models based on games, bets, or known probabilities are applied to complex real-world systems without justification.
fallacies.body: Models based on games, bets, or known probabilities are applied to complex real-world systems without justification. Real events often have unknown distributions, changing rules, feedback, and nonrandom agents.

examples.text: Because a casino game has a known house edge, the same calculation proves a city's housing market will behave predictably.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument imports a toy model's assumptions into an open system without testing them.
doesNotCountWhen: A game model is useful when the real process genuinely satisfies its fixed probabilities and independence assumptions.

fallacies.name: Lump-of-labour fallacy
fallacies.summary: The amount of work in an economy is assumed fixed, so one group's employment must reduce another's by the same amount.
fallacies.body: The amount of work in an economy is assumed fixed, so one group's employment must reduce another's by the same amount. Demand, productivity, investment, and new tasks can change total employment opportunities.

examples.text: If immigrants take 10,000 jobs, exactly 10,000 native workers must lose jobs permanently.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion treats labor demand as a fixed finite quantity without considering wage, output, or market adjustment.
doesNotCountWhen: A fixed labor quantity may apply to a narrowly defined short-term task allocation under explicit constraints.

fallacies.name: Magical thinking as causal inference
fallacies.summary: An unrelated ritual, wish, or symbolic act is treated as causing an external outcome.
fallacies.body: An unrelated ritual, wish, or symbolic act is treated as causing an external outcome. Similarity, intention, or temporal coincidence does not supply a causal mechanism.

examples.text: I wore my lucky socks and won, so the socks caused the victory.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The alleged cause has no plausible mechanism and is supported only by ritual association or coincidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A symbolic act can be causally relevant when it changes human behavior or another mediating condition.

fallacies.name: McNamara fallacy
fallacies.summary: Only what is easily measured is considered, while unmeasured factors crucial to the decision are ignored.
fallacies.body: Only what is easily measured is considered, while unmeasured factors crucial to the decision are ignored. Measurement availability is not the same as importance or evidential relevance.

examples.text: The campaign counted enemy vehicles destroyed and ignored civilian support, so the rising score proves victory.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The decision rule excludes qualitative, hidden, or hard-to-measure variables solely because they lack convenient numbers.
doesNotCountWhen: Quantitative focus is sound when the measured variables are shown to capture the decision's relevant outcomes.

fallacies.name: Middle-ground fallacy
fallacies.summary: A compromise position is assumed true or best merely because it lies between two opposed positions.
fallacies.body: A compromise position is assumed true or best merely because it lies between two opposed positions. Truth and optimal policy do not necessarily occupy the numerical or rhetorical midpoint.

examples.text: One doctor recommends no exercise and another recommends daily exercise, so exercising every other day must be medically correct.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument treats the midpoint between claims as justified without independent evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A middle position is warranted when evidence or constraints specifically support it.

fallacies.name: Misleading vividness
fallacies.summary: A vivid anecdote or image is given more evidential weight than representative but less memorable data.
fallacies.body: A vivid anecdote or image is given more evidential weight than representative but less memorable data. Emotional salience affects recall, not the underlying frequency or probability.

examples.text: After hearing one graphic shark-attack story, a traveler concludes that swimming is more dangerous than driving.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A single memorable case overrides base rates or a larger relevant dataset without justification.
doesNotCountWhen: A vivid case is relevant when it illustrates a previously established pattern or supplies unique direct evidence.

fallacies.name: Missing-data fallacy
fallacies.summary: Absence of reported or available data is treated as evidence for a preferred conclusion.
fallacies.body: Absence of reported or available data is treated as evidence for a preferred conclusion. Missingness can result from sampling, measurement, reporting, or selection processes unrelated to the hypothesis.

examples.text: The audit found no complaints, so the service caused no harm even though complaints were never collected.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument interprets an unobserved value as a favorable observed value without analyzing why it is missing.
doesNotCountWhen: Absence can support a claim when the observation system was designed to detect the event reliably.

fallacies.name: Modal scope fallacy
fallacies.summary: Confusing the necessity of an implication with the necessity of its consequent.
fallacies.body: Confusing the necessity of an implication with the necessity of its consequent. Even if P → Q is necessary, a contingent truth of P establishes Q at the actual world without making Q true in every possible world.

examples.text: It is necessary that if Alex is a bachelor then Alex is unmarried. Alex is a bachelor. Therefore, Alex is necessarily unmarried.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The form □(P → Q), P, therefore □Q lacks a premise establishing that P is necessary.
doesNotCountWhen: In normal modal systems, necessary implication together with necessary P supports necessary Q; ordinary Q also follows from the original premises in reflexive frames.

fallacies.name: Moralistic fallacy
fallacies.summary: A belief about how things ought to be is used as evidence that they are that way.
fallacies.body: A belief about how things ought to be is used as evidence that they are that way. Moral approval or disapproval does not determine empirical facts.

examples.text: People deserve equal opportunity, so differences in every occupational outcome cannot have any biological contribution.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A normative judgment is presented as a factual description or causal constraint.
doesNotCountWhen: A moral premise may guide action or motivate investigation without being used as empirical proof.

fallacies.name: Motte-and-bailey
fallacies.summary: A controversial strong claim is defended by retreating to a weaker defensible claim, then the strong claim is resumed without new support.
fallacies.body: A controversial strong claim is defended by retreating to a weaker defensible claim, then the strong claim is resumed without new support. Evidence for the modest position does not establish the broader position.

examples.text: The writer argues that technology controls society, retreats to saying technology influences society when challenged, then claims the original thesis survived.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker alternates between an ambitious claim and a less controversial one while treating them as interchangeable.
doesNotCountWhen: A position is sound when the speaker clearly distinguishes the claims and supplies separate support for each.

fallacies.name: Moving the goalposts
fallacies.summary: The required evidence for accepting a claim is changed after the offered evidence meets the previous requirement.
fallacies.body: The required evidence for accepting a claim is changed after the offered evidence meets the previous requirement. Changing standards opportunistically makes the claim unfalsifiable by ordinary inquiry.

examples.text: After the experiment succeeds, the skeptic demands a larger sample, then a different laboratory, without explaining the new standard beforehand.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The acceptance criterion is raised or altered only in response to evidence that previously satisfied it.
doesNotCountWhen: A revised standard is legitimate when new risks, errors, or scope are explicitly justified independently of the result.

fallacies.name: Multiple-comparisons fallacy
fallacies.summary: Many hypotheses or comparisons are tested but only a chance favorable result is reported as decisive.
fallacies.body: Many hypotheses or comparisons are tested but only a chance favorable result is reported as decisive. Repeated testing increases false-positive probability unless the analysis accounts for multiplicity.

examples.text: A researcher tests 100 outcomes and publishes the one with p=.04 as proof that the treatment works.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion highlights an uncorrected significant result from a large search over possible comparisons.
doesNotCountWhen: A result is credible when comparisons were preregistered or multiplicity was controlled and transparently reported.

fallacies.name: Name-calling as refutation
fallacies.summary: A derogatory label is used in place of a reason against a person's claim.
fallacies.body: A derogatory label is used in place of a reason against a person's claim. Insulting a speaker does not show that the proposition is false.

examples.text: Only an idiot would oppose the zoning plan, so the zoning plan is correct.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The alleged defect is a slur or status label unrelated to the truth of the target claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Character evidence is relevant when the claim concerns the person's conduct or reliability and is supported specifically.

fallacies.name: Naturalistic fallacy
fallacies.summary: In Moore's terminology, identifying goodness with a natural or other independently specified property as though that settled what goodness is.
fallacies.body: In Moore's terminology, identifying goodness with a natural or other independently specified property as though that settled what goodness is. Moore argued that identifying pleasure with goodness leaves open whether pleasure is good; his argument and rejection of ethical naturalism remain disputed. This differs from the appeal to nature and the is–ought gap.

examples.text: Good simply means pleasant, so asking whether a pleasant experience is good asks nothing beyond whether it is pleasant.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A proposed account of goodness equates it with another property while treating substantive questions about value as settled by that identity.
doesNotCountWhen: Defending ethical naturalism with substantive arguments is a live philosophical position, not a demonstrated logical mistake merely because Moore rejected it.

fallacies.name: Negating antecedent and consequent
fallacies.summary: Inferring ¬P → ¬Q from P → Q by negating both sides without reversing their order.
fallacies.body: Inferring ¬P → ¬Q from P → Q by negating both sides without reversing their order. From P → Q, contraposition gives ¬Q → ¬P; the inverse ¬P → ¬Q need not hold.

examples.text: If the switch is pressed, the lamp lights. Therefore, if the switch is not pressed, the lamp does not light, although a timer can also turn it on.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A conditional P → Q is replaced by its inverse ¬P → ¬Q without justification.
doesNotCountWhen: The inverse follows when the original relationship is biconditional; using the contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P is already valid.

fallacies.name: Negative conclusion from affirmative premises
fallacies.summary: A categorical syllogism draws a negative conclusion from two affirmative premises.
fallacies.body: A categorical syllogism draws a negative conclusion from two affirmative premises. Two affirmative categorical premises do not establish exclusion between their terms in the standard syllogistic system.

examples.text: All poets are artists; all artists are dreamers; therefore no poets are dreamers.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Both premises are affirmative but the conclusion denies the relation between its terms.
doesNotCountWhen: A negative conclusion can be valid when at least one premise is negative and the syllogism satisfies the other rules.

fallacies.name: Nirvana fallacy
fallacies.summary: A real proposal is rejected because it is not perfect or because an imagined ideal would be better.
fallacies.body: A real proposal is rejected because it is not perfect or because an imagined ideal would be better. Policy comparison should use feasible alternatives and relevant tradeoffs, not perfection as the baseline.

examples.text: The vaccine is useless because it prevents 90 percent rather than 100 percent of infections.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument compares an imperfect option with an unattainable flawless alternative.
doesNotCountWhen: Rejecting an option is rational when its harms, costs, or failures exceed those of feasible alternatives.

fallacies.name: No true Scotsman
fallacies.summary: A universal claim is protected from a counterexample by redefining the group to exclude the counterexample.
fallacies.body: A universal claim is protected from a counterexample by redefining the group to exclude the counterexample. Ad hoc redefinition makes the original generalization immune to evidence.

examples.text: No environmentalist supports nuclear power; when Maya does, she is told that a true environmentalist would not.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A counterexample is dismissed by adding an unsupported purity condition after the fact.
doesNotCountWhen: A group definition is legitimate when its criteria were stated independently and apply consistently.

fallacies.name: Non sequitur
fallacies.summary: The conclusion does not follow from the premises even though it may be rhetorically adjacent.
fallacies.body: The conclusion does not follow from the premises even though it may be rhetorically adjacent. A gap in logical relevance cannot be repaired by confidence or sequence.

examples.text: The library is quiet, and the moon is full, so the tax proposal should pass.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument supplies premises that leave the conclusion's truth unchanged across plausible cases.
doesNotCountWhen: A conclusion is not a non sequitur when an omitted but established premise supplies the connection.

fallacies.name: Non-recognition fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating refusal to acknowledge an unwelcome fact as a reason that its consequences can be ignored.
fallacies.body: Treating refusal to acknowledge an unwelcome fact as a reason that its consequences can be ignored. This nonstandard rhetoric label concerns confusing recognition with creation or endorsement. Describing an event accurately need not legitimize it, and denying its description does not remove its effects.

examples.text: We refuse to acknowledge that the competitor launched its product, so our sales forecast need not account for it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An actor's refusal to recognize a fact substitutes for assessing evidence that it exists or matters.
doesNotCountWhen: Diplomatic or legal non-recognition can be a policy position without denying the underlying factual situation.

fallacies.name: Notable-effort fallacy
fallacies.summary: Effort or sacrifice is treated as evidence that the resulting claim, plan, or product is correct or valuable.
fallacies.body: Effort or sacrifice is treated as evidence that the resulting claim, plan, or product is correct or valuable. Work invested does not guarantee quality, truth, or effectiveness.

examples.text: The committee spent two years designing the policy, so the policy must reduce poverty.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument cites time, hardship, or dedication instead of results or reasons bearing on the claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Effort is relevant when the task is itself being evaluated or when it provides evidence of process quality without being treated as conclusive.

fallacies.name: Nutpicking
fallacies.summary: The weakest or most eccentric examples from an opposing group are selected to represent the whole group.
fallacies.body: The weakest or most eccentric examples from an opposing group are selected to represent the whole group. Outliers do not establish what the broader group believes or does.

examples.text: One fringe post denies the moon landing, so all climate scientists reject basic evidence.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument searches an opponent's large population for absurd examples and generalizes from them.
doesNotCountWhen: Criticizing a specific fringe member is fair when the claim is explicitly about that member rather than the group.

fallacies.name: Obscurum per obscurius
fallacies.summary: An obscure claim is explained by an even more obscure claim, creating an appearance of explanation without increased understanding.
fallacies.body: An obscure claim is explained by an even more obscure claim, creating an appearance of explanation without increased understanding. An explanation must reduce uncertainty rather than replace one mystery with another.

examples.text: The patient is ill because of a dyscratic vital force whose imbalance causes illness.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The proposed explanation uses undefined, equally opaque, or more technical-sounding terms with no testable mechanism.
doesNotCountWhen: Technical terminology is explanatory when its terms are independently defined and connect to observable mechanisms.

fallacies.name: Overexplanation
fallacies.summary: Using excessive detail to obscure the inferential gap or burden the audience instead of supporting a conclusion.
fallacies.body: Using excessive detail to obscure the inferential gap or burden the audience instead of supporting a conclusion. This rhetoric label describes a communication tactic rather than an inherently invalid logical form. Detail becomes problematic when volume is treated as proof or makes the relevant supporting step harder to examine.

examples.text: Asked why a payment was authorized, an official recites the department's entire history but never identifies the authorization.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Excessive information substitutes for the missing reason or impedes examination of it.
doesNotCountWhen: A long explanation can be necessary when a complex issue genuinely requires the detail.

fallacies.name: Overextended analogy
fallacies.summary: An analogy is carried beyond the shared features that make it useful, and its unsupported details are treated as conclusions.
fallacies.body: An analogy is carried beyond the shared features that make it useful, and its unsupported details are treated as conclusions. Analogies illuminate selected relations but do not preserve every property across domains.

examples.text: Because a state is like a household, it should balance its budget exactly like a family and never borrow for infrastructure.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument imports additional relations from the source case without showing that they hold in the target case.
doesNotCountWhen: An analogy is sound when its scope is limited to identified correspondences relevant to the conclusion.

fallacies.name: Overextended outrage
fallacies.summary: Moral outrage at one instance is generalized into condemnation of every related case or person.
fallacies.body: Moral outrage at one instance is generalized into condemnation of every related case or person. A shocking example does not establish that all cases share its culpability or severity.

examples.text: One charity executive stole donations, so every charity executive is a criminal exploiter.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument lets emotional condemnation of a salient case replace case-specific evidence across a wider class.
doesNotCountWhen: Broader condemnation is justified when representative evidence establishes a systematic pattern.

fallacies.name: Overgeneralization
fallacies.summary: A conclusion is extended from some cases or a limited context to all cases without adequate warrant.
fallacies.body: A conclusion is extended from some cases or a limited context to all cases without adequate warrant. The scope of the conclusion exceeds the scope of the evidence.

examples.text: This software failed during one update, so software updates are always unreliable.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A local, conditional, or occasional observation is converted into an unrestricted universal claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Generalization is acceptable when the evidence and stated conditions cover the broader scope.

fallacies.name: Overwhelming exception
fallacies.summary: A rule is defended by dismissing so many counterexamples that the claimed rule becomes empty or trivial.
fallacies.body: A rule is defended by dismissing so many counterexamples that the claimed rule becomes empty or trivial. A rule that survives only by excluding its ordinary cases has lost explanatory content.

examples.text: All managers support the policy, except the managers who oppose it, who are not real managers.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Exceptions are repeatedly added ad hoc until contrary evidence no longer counts.
doesNotCountWhen: Exceptions are legitimate when independently defined, limited, and consistent with the rule's intended scope.

fallacies.name: Package-deal fallacy
fallacies.summary: Several distinct ideas are bundled under one label so that accepting one pressures acceptance of the others.
fallacies.body: Several distinct ideas are bundled under one label so that accepting one pressures acceptance of the others. Conjoined concepts may require different evidence and can be evaluated separately.

examples.text: If you support public schools, you support bureaucracy, indoctrination, and waste.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A loaded phrase links a defensible component to disputed components without arguing for each connection.
doesNotCountWhen: A package is legitimate when its elements are explicitly interdependent by definition or causal structure.

fallacies.name: Pathetic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Human feelings or intentions are attributed to inanimate things and then used as explanatory evidence.
fallacies.body: Human feelings or intentions are attributed to inanimate things and then used as explanatory evidence. Metaphorical personification does not establish literal agency or causation.

examples.text: The storm was angry at the town, so it destroyed the harbor as punishment.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A poetic description of nature's emotion is treated as a factual account of why an event occurred.
doesNotCountWhen: Personification is harmless when clearly metaphorical and not used as literal evidence.

fallacies.name: Persuasive definition
fallacies.summary: A term is defined with commendatory or condemnatory wording to make the associated conclusion seem true by definition.
fallacies.body: A term is defined with commendatory or condemnatory wording to make the associated conclusion seem true by definition. Emotive stipulation cannot settle a substantive dispute about the thing being named.

examples.text: A real patriot is anyone who supports this bill, so opposition to the bill is unpatriotic.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The definition embeds the speaker's verdict in a disputed term and then reasons from that verdict.
doesNotCountWhen: A definition is legitimate when it is openly stipulative for a clear purpose and not presented as an independent factual conclusion.

fallacies.name: Poisoning the well
fallacies.summary: A target is discredited in advance so that anything the target says will be rejected regardless of its content.
fallacies.body: A target is discredited in advance so that anything the target says will be rejected regardless of its content. Preemptive suspicion does not evaluate the actual reasons or evidence.

examples.text: Before the witness testifies, the prosecutor says she is a notorious liar, so no statement she makes can be believed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The audience is told to discount a source before hearing the source's particular claim or evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A warning is relevant when it presents specific, verified reliability problems and leaves each claim open to evaluation.

fallacies.name: Political-correctness fallacy
fallacies.summary: A claim is rejected or accepted solely because it conforms to or violates a prevailing rule of polite or approved expression.
fallacies.body: A claim is rejected or accepted solely because it conforms to or violates a prevailing rule of polite or approved expression. Language norms do not by themselves establish the truth of the underlying proposition.

examples.text: The term is politically incorrect, so the reported disparity cannot be real.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument treats acceptability of wording or ideology as decisive evidence for the factual claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Language criticism is legitimate when the wording is inaccurate, harmful, or obstructs the stated communicative purpose.

fallacies.name: Possibility-to-certainty fallacy
fallacies.summary: Because a proposition is possible, it is treated as certain or highly probable.
fallacies.body: Because a proposition is possible, it is treated as certain or highly probable. Possibility requires only a compatible scenario and does not establish likelihood.

examples.text: The sensor could have malfunctioned, so it definitely did malfunction.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument moves from could or might to must, certainly, or an equivalent confidence level without new evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is justified when additional evidence raises the possibility to the claimed probability or certainty.

fallacies.name: Post hoc ergo propter hoc
fallacies.summary: Because one event followed another, the earlier event is declared the cause of the later event.
fallacies.body: Because one event followed another, the earlier event is declared the cause of the later event. Sequence alone cannot distinguish causation from coincidence, common cause, or reversal.

examples.text: The mayor took office before unemployment fell, so the mayor's election caused the recovery.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The only causal support is that the alleged cause occurred first or immediately before the effect.
doesNotCountWhen: Temporal order supports a causal hypothesis when combined with mechanism, controls, and comparison.

fallacies.name: Pragmatic fallacy
fallacies.summary: A claim is treated as true because believing or asserting it would be useful, comforting, or socially convenient.
fallacies.body: A claim is treated as true because believing or asserting it would be useful, comforting, or socially convenient. Utility of belief does not determine correspondence with reality.

examples.text: It would be disastrous if the bridge were unsafe, so the bridge must be safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument cites desirable consequences of a proposition as evidence for its truth.
doesNotCountWhen: Practical consequences can rationally guide action or inquiry when they are not mistaken for truth evidence.

fallacies.name: Prejudicial language
fallacies.summary: Loaded wording is used to bias judgment about a subject instead of supplying relevant reasons.
fallacies.body: Loaded wording is used to bias judgment about a subject instead of supplying relevant reasons. Emotional connotations can influence acceptance without changing the facts.

examples.text: The greedy tax-grabber wants to seize your hard-earned money, so the tax proposal is wrong.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The description embeds praise or blame that would disappear under neutral wording while the alleged support remains unchanged.
doesNotCountWhen: Strong language is legitimate when it accurately describes documented conduct and is not substituted for the argument's reasons.

fallacies.name: Presuming truth from lack of disproof
fallacies.summary: A claim is treated as true because no one has disproved it.
fallacies.body: A claim is treated as true because no one has disproved it. Failure to refute a claim is not evidence for it when the burden of proof lies with the claimant.

examples.text: No one has proved that the abandoned mine is not haunted, so it is haunted.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument cites absence of a disproof while offering no positive evidence and no reason that disproof should already exist.
doesNotCountWhen: Lack of disproof supports provisional acceptance only when a reliable search would almost certainly have found disconfirming evidence and the burden is appropriately assigned.

fallacies.name: Proof by intimidation
fallacies.summary: It treats confidence, status, or threats as substitutes for an argument's missing support.
fallacies.body: It treats confidence, status, or threats as substitutes for an argument's missing support. Pressure can affect compliance without making the conclusion follow from the premises.

examples.text: The professor says, "Anyone who doubts my theorem is incompetent," so the theorem must be true.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker relies on ridicule, authority, or retaliation instead of answering the stated objection.
doesNotCountWhen: Forceful presentation accompanies independently sufficient reasons and is not offered as their support.

fallacies.name: Proof surrogate
fallacies.summary: It presents a citation, label, calculation, or procedural artifact as if it were the proof of the conclusion.
fallacies.body: It presents a citation, label, calculation, or procedural artifact as if it were the proof of the conclusion. A surrogate may indicate evidence exists, but it does not establish the relevant inferential link by itself.

examples.text: The report has a regression table, so its claim that the policy caused the recovery is proven.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The supposed proof is named or displayed while the needed premises or derivation are omitted.
doesNotCountWhen: The cited source or calculation is explained and actually entails or materially supports the conclusion.

fallacies.name: Prosecutor's fallacy
fallacies.summary: It confuses the probability of the evidence given innocence with the probability of innocence given the evidence.
fallacies.body: It confuses the probability of the evidence given innocence with the probability of innocence given the evidence. A rare observation among innocent people does not by itself show that an accused person is probably guilty without a prior probability and alternatives.

examples.text: Only one in a million innocent people match the DNA profile, so there is only a one-in-a-million chance the defendant is innocent.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument reverses a conditional likelihood and ignores base rates or the size of the innocent population.
doesNotCountWhen: The conclusion uses a valid posterior calculation with an explicit prior and relevant competing hypotheses.

fallacies.name: Psychogenetic fallacy
fallacies.summary: It rejects or accepts a belief solely because of the psychological process that produced it.
fallacies.body: It rejects or accepts a belief solely because of the psychological process that produced it. A belief's origin may explain why someone holds it, but truth depends on its content and evidence.

examples.text: Mara believes the theorem because of childhood praise, so the theorem is false.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument attacks the belief's psychological cause instead of assessing its truth-making evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Psychological origins are relevant when the claim concerns causes, reliability, or testimony formation.

fallacies.name: Quantifier-shift fallacy
fallacies.summary: It illicitly moves a quantifier across a relation, replacing different witnesses with one common witness.
fallacies.body: It illicitly moves a quantifier across a relation, replacing different witnesses with one common witness. The existence of a suitable object for each subject does not imply one object suits every subject.

examples.text: Every student admires some author; therefore, there is an author admired by every student.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion changes the scope or dependency of quantifiers without a valid argument for the stronger claim.
doesNotCountWhen: The quantifier movement is licensed by additional premises such as a specified common object.

fallacies.name: Quantum-physics fallacy
