fallacies.summary: It invokes quantum terminology to make an unsupported claim about ordinary-scale minds, choices, or events.
fallacies.body: It invokes quantum terminology to make an unsupported claim about ordinary-scale minds, choices, or events. Quantum phenomena do not automatically supply evidence for a proposed macroscopic conclusion.

examples.text: Particles can be in superposition, so a person can simultaneously have and not have a settled contractual obligation.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Quantum words are used as the main bridge from microscopic physics to an unrelated conclusion without a physical model.
doesNotCountWhen: A qualified claim follows from an actual quantum theory, experiment, and scale-appropriate application.

fallacies.name: Questionable premise
fallacies.summary: It treats a premise whose truth is disputed or unsupported as established for the purpose of its conclusion.
fallacies.body: It treats a premise whose truth is disputed or unsupported as established for the purpose of its conclusion. An argument can be valid in form while failing to justify a premise that carries its conclusion.

examples.text: Because all dreams predict the future, the dream warned that the bridge would collapse.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A controversial factual or normative premise is asserted without evidence or acknowledgment of its contestability.
doesNotCountWhen: The premise is independently supported, stipulated, or explicitly presented as a conditional assumption.

fallacies.name: Quoting out of context
fallacies.summary: It uses a fragment of a statement after removing surrounding words that change its meaning or qualification.
fallacies.body: It uses a fragment of a statement after removing surrounding words that change its meaning or qualification. The omitted context can reverse, limit, or otherwise alter what the speaker asserted.

examples.text: The minister said, "The plan is not safe," but the full sentence was "The plan is not safe without inspections," so the quote proves opposition to inspections.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The quoted words support a different claim than the complete passage supports because relevant context is omitted.
doesNotCountWhen: The excerpt preserves the relevant scope, qualifiers, speaker, time, and surrounding meaning.

fallacies.name: Red herring
fallacies.summary: It diverts attention to an irrelevant issue in order to avoid the question under discussion.
fallacies.body: It diverts attention to an irrelevant issue in order to avoid the question under discussion. A true side issue cannot answer the original claim merely by changing the subject.

examples.text: Asked whether the bridge is structurally sound, the mayor describes how attractive its new lights are.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response changes the topic and supplies no premise relevant to the disputed conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: The apparently tangential point reveals a premise or consequence that is genuinely relevant to the original issue.

fallacies.name: Reductio ad Hitlerum
fallacies.summary: It rejects a proposal because Hitler or the Nazis supported a similar proposal.
fallacies.body: It rejects a proposal because Hitler or the Nazis supported a similar proposal. Historical association does not determine whether the proposal is true or beneficial.

examples.text: Hitler promoted physical fitness, so public exercise programs are morally wrong.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion depends on Nazi or Hitler association rather than the proposal's own evidence and merits.
doesNotCountWhen: The historical comparison supplies relevant evidence about a specific policy's consequences or ideology rather than mere guilt by association.

fallacies.name: Regression fallacy
fallacies.summary: It attributes a change after an extreme result to an intervention while ignoring regression toward the mean.
fallacies.body: It attributes a change after an extreme result to an intervention while ignoring regression toward the mean. Extreme observations tend to be followed by less extreme ones even without treatment.

examples.text: After the worst migraine of the year, Lena takes a bracelet and improves, proving the bracelet cured her.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An extreme baseline is selected, a natural return is observed, and causal evidence for the intervention is absent or weak.
doesNotCountWhen: A controlled comparison, repeated evidence, or mechanism supports an effect beyond expected regression.

fallacies.name: Reification
fallacies.summary: It treats an abstraction, relationship, or model as a concrete agent or object with its own causal powers.
fallacies.body: It treats an abstraction, relationship, or model as a concrete agent or object with its own causal powers. A useful concept does not thereby become a physical or intentional entity.

examples.text: The average voter demanded the law, so the numerical average personally made the demand.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A noun for a population, property, or model is assigned literal agency or object-like behavior without justification.
doesNotCountWhen: The term refers to a real entity under an explicitly defined institutional or scientific model.

fallacies.name: Relative privation
fallacies.summary: It dismisses a genuine deprivation because someone else is worse off.
fallacies.body: It dismisses a genuine deprivation because someone else is worse off. Comparative disadvantage does not remove the relevant harm or unmet need.

examples.text: Workers should not complain about unsafe temperatures because disaster victims have lost their homes.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A worse-off comparison is used to conclude that the first condition is not a real problem or does not merit remedy.
doesNotCountWhen: The comparison is relevant to triage, resource allocation, or proportional priority without denying the first harm.

fallacies.name: Reverse causation
fallacies.summary: It infers that an observed association has the causal direction opposite to the one supported by the evidence.
fallacies.body: It infers that an observed association has the causal direction opposite to the one supported by the evidence. Correlation alone does not identify which variable causes which, and an outcome can cause its apparent predictor.

examples.text: People with umbrellas are more likely to be wet, so carrying umbrellas makes people wet.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument treats an effect or consequence as the cause of its correlated condition without temporal or mechanistic support.
doesNotCountWhen: Temporal order, intervention, or a causal model independently supports the proposed direction.

fallacies.name: Righteousness fallacy
fallacies.summary: It infers that a claim or action is correct because the speaker's cause is morally righteous.
fallacies.body: It infers that a claim or action is correct because the speaker's cause is morally righteous. Moral commitment does not make factual premises true or make an invalid inference valid.

examples.text: Our campaign fights corruption, so every statistic in our campaign must be accurate.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker's declared virtue is offered as support for an unrelated factual or logical conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: The moral aim is connected through independently supported premises and does not replace them.

fallacies.name: Rights-to-ought fallacy
fallacies.summary: It infers that because someone has a right or permission, exercising it is necessarily obligatory or wise.
fallacies.body: It infers that because someone has a right or permission, exercising it is necessarily obligatory or wise. A permission or entitlement sets a constraint on others but does not settle every prudential or moral choice.

examples.text: You have a right to publish the data, so you ought to publish it immediately despite the privacy risk.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument changes a claim about what may be done into a claim about what must or should be done without further premises.
doesNotCountWhen: Additional duties, consequences, or context establish the obligation beyond the mere right.

fallacies.name: Scapegoating
fallacies.summary: It assigns blame for a complex outcome to a convenient person or group without adequate causal evidence.
fallacies.body: It assigns blame for a complex outcome to a convenient person or group without adequate causal evidence. Complex outcomes commonly have multiple causes, and social blame can be selected for convenience rather than explanation.

examples.text: Rent rose because immigrants moved here, although zoning, interest rates, and demand also changed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A disliked or vulnerable target is blamed as the principal cause while relevant alternatives and evidence are ignored.
doesNotCountWhen: Evidence identifies the target as a substantial cause and the claim does not rely on group hostility or oversimplification.

fallacies.name: Self-righteousness fallacy
fallacies.summary: It treats one's own moral certainty or purity as proof that one's accusation or conclusion is correct.
fallacies.body: It treats one's own moral certainty or purity as proof that one's accusation or conclusion is correct. Feeling morally superior does not establish facts or answer objections.

examples.text: I would never cheat, so my accusation that the accountant falsified the ledger must be true.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker's asserted virtue is the primary support for a disputed conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: The conclusion is supported by records, witnesses, or other independent evidence in addition to moral character.

fallacies.name: Self-sealing argument
fallacies.summary: It is constructed so that no possible observation can count against it, often by treating disconfirmation as confirmation.
fallacies.body: It is constructed so that no possible observation can count against it, often by treating disconfirmation as confirmation. An assertion insulated from all possible counterevidence cannot be empirically tested.

examples.text: If the amulet works, it protects you; if it fails, your skepticism blocked its power, so every outcome proves it works.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument supplies an ad hoc reinterpretation that makes both confirming and disconfirming outcomes support the claim.
doesNotCountWhen: The claim states conditions under which it would be rejected and permits evidence to lower confidence.

fallacies.name: Self-selection fallacy
fallacies.summary: It generalizes from people who chose to participate or appear, treating them as representative of the wider population.
fallacies.body: It generalizes from people who chose to participate or appear, treating them as representative of the wider population. Voluntary participation can correlate with the outcome and create selection bias.

examples.text: An online poll of people who chose to discuss taxes shows that 80 percent of citizens support the tax.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The sample enters through self-selection and the conclusion is extended to a population without correcting for selection.
doesNotCountWhen: A probability sample or valid adjustment establishes representativeness for the target population.

fallacies.name: Shifting the burden of proof
fallacies.summary: It demands that an opponent disprove the speaker's unsupported claim instead of supplying support for it.
fallacies.body: It demands that an opponent disprove the speaker's unsupported claim instead of supplying support for it. The person making a positive assertion carries the initial burden of evidence.

examples.text: I say the museum hides a dragon; unless you prove there is no dragon, my claim stands.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument treats lack of disproof as evidence or makes the challenger establish the universal negative.
doesNotCountWhen: The claim is supported by evidence, or a party appropriately bears a burden created by a prior established showing.

fallacies.name: Shoehorning
fallacies.summary: It forces evidence or a case into a familiar category despite important mismatches.
fallacies.body: It forces evidence or a case into a familiar category despite important mismatches. A label can simplify analysis only when the defining features actually fit.

examples.text: The software has a settings menu, so it is a spreadsheet and must be evaluated by spreadsheet formulas.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The classification is defended by one superficial similarity while contrary defining features are ignored.
doesNotCountWhen: The category is used provisionally and the relevant criteria, limits, and mismatches are addressed.

fallacies.name: Simpleton's fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating a complex issue as settled by an oversimplified slogan or by feigned inability to understand qualifications.
fallacies.body: Treating a complex issue as settled by an oversimplified slogan or by feigned inability to understand qualifications. This label has inconsistent uses in rhetoric catalogs and is not a standard formal fallacy. The relevant defect must be identified specifically, such as ignoring an indispensable distinction while claiming decisive simplicity.

examples.text: All borrowing is bad, so there is no need to compare the costs and returns of this investment loan.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An oversimplified formulation is used to dismiss distinctions needed for the actual conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: Asking for a clear explanation of a complex claim is legitimate and can expose real problems.

fallacies.name: Slippery-slope fallacy
fallacies.summary: It claims that permitting a first step will inevitably produce an extreme outcome through an unsupported chain of events.
fallacies.body: It claims that permitting a first step will inevitably produce an extreme outcome through an unsupported chain of events. Each link needs evidence; possibility alone does not establish inevitability or high probability.

examples.text: If the city allows one food truck, soon every street will be restaurants and no homes will remain.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument predicts a sequence of escalating consequences without supported links or effective stopping points.
doesNotCountWhen: Evidence shows the links are likely and no credible safeguards or stopping conditions prevent the result.

fallacies.name: Small-sample fallacy
fallacies.summary: It draws a broad conclusion from too few observations to estimate the relevant population reliably.
fallacies.body: It draws a broad conclusion from too few observations to estimate the relevant population reliably. Small samples have high uncertainty and can be dominated by chance or unusual cases.

examples.text: Two tourists from Norland were rude, so Norlanders are rude.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The sample is too small for the precision and generality claimed, with no adequate uncertainty analysis.
doesNotCountWhen: The claim is explicitly limited to the observed cases or a justified design makes the small sample informative.

fallacies.name: Special pleading
fallacies.summary: It exempts a favored case from a general rule without a relevant distinction.
fallacies.body: It exempts a favored case from a general rule without a relevant distinction. An exception requires a principled reason that applies to the rule's purpose, not mere preference.

examples.text: Everyone must disclose gifts except the mayor, because her office is important.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker applies a rule to comparable cases but invents an unsupported exception for the preferred case.
doesNotCountWhen: A relevant legal, causal, or normative distinction independently justifies the exception.

fallacies.name: Spin doctoring
fallacies.summary: It selectively frames true information to create a misleading impression about the underlying result.
fallacies.body: It selectively frames true information to create a misleading impression about the underlying result. Literal truth can mislead when material context, comparisons, or uncertainty are strategically omitted.

examples.text: The company reports record sales while omitting that inflation-adjusted sales fell and returns doubled.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The presentation emphasizes favorable facts and suppresses material unfavorable context to steer interpretation.
doesNotCountWhen: The framing is balanced, context is disclosed, and the stated conclusion follows from the complete relevant evidence.

fallacies.name: Spiritual fallacy
fallacies.summary: It uses a spiritual or mystical assertion as evidence for a conclusion without a justified connection.
fallacies.body: It uses a spiritual or mystical assertion as evidence for a conclusion without a justified connection. Spiritual significance or personal revelation is not automatically public evidence for an external claim.

examples.text: My ancestors approve this investment, so the company cannot lose money.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An unverifiable spiritual source is treated as decisive support for a factual, predictive, or normative conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: The claim is explicitly personal or faith-based, or independently testable evidence supports the external conclusion.

fallacies.name: Spotlight fallacy
fallacies.summary: It treats a salient or publicly discussed case as if it represented the frequency or importance of the whole population.
fallacies.body: It treats a salient or publicly discussed case as if it represented the frequency or importance of the whole population. Attention is not proportional to prevalence because unusual cases receive disproportionate coverage.

examples.text: News reports three shark attacks, so swimming at this beach is usually deadly.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A vivid, recent, or heavily reported case is used to estimate a broader rate without denominator data.
doesNotCountWhen: Representative statistics or a defined scope support the generalization, and salience is not its evidence.

fallacies.name: Stolen-concept fallacy
fallacies.summary: It uses a concept while denying or attacking a more fundamental concept required for that use.
fallacies.body: It uses a concept while denying or attacking a more fundamental concept required for that use. The denial undermines the conditions that make the speaker's own claim meaningful or possible.

examples.text: There are no objective truths, and that statement is objectively true for everyone.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion presupposes the validity, existence, or authority of what it explicitly rejects.
doesNotCountWhen: The concepts are used in distinct senses or the alleged dependence is not actually required.

fallacies.name: Straw man
fallacies.summary: It refutes a weaker or distorted version of an opponent's actual position instead of that position.
fallacies.body: It refutes a weaker or distorted version of an opponent's actual position instead of that position. Defeating a misrepresentation gives no evidence against the original claim.

examples.text: A proposal for targeted subsidies is dismissed as a plan to give everyone unlimited money.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The reply replaces the opponent's stated view with an easier claim that lacks its qualifications or scope.
doesNotCountWhen: The reconstructed version is charitable, accurate, and then separately criticized with relevant reasons.

fallacies.name: Style over substance
fallacies.summary: It treats polished presentation, eloquence, credentials, or formatting as evidence that the underlying claim is true.
fallacies.body: It treats polished presentation, eloquence, credentials, or formatting as evidence that the underlying claim is true. Presentation can affect perception without improving the claim's evidence.

examples.text: The glossy investment deck uses expert fonts and confident prose, so its forecast must be reliable.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Aesthetic or rhetorical quality is the principal support for a factual or logical conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: Style is used only for communication while the conclusion rests on independently assessed evidence.

fallacies.name: Subjectivist fallacy
fallacies.summary: It concludes that a claim has no objective truth merely because people disagree or because judgments can be personal.
fallacies.body: It concludes that a claim has no objective truth merely because people disagree or because judgments can be personal. Disagreement or subjective preference does not eliminate objective facts or standards where they apply.

examples.text: People disagree about the dosage, so there is no fact about which dosage is safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument moves from variation in beliefs or tastes to the nonexistence of objective truth.
doesNotCountWhen: The subject is genuinely preference-dependent or the evidence establishes an appropriate relativist framework.

fallacies.name: Subverted support
fallacies.summary: It presents evidence whose reliability, relevance, or interpretation is undermined by the same argument or source supplying it.
fallacies.body: It presents evidence whose reliability, relevance, or interpretation is undermined by the same argument or source supplying it. Evidence cannot support a conclusion when its stated basis defeats its credibility or applicability.

examples.text: The anonymous survey proves voters support the plan, but every respondent was paid by the campaign to answer yes.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The supporting item contains a disclosed defect that removes its probative force, yet the conclusion still relies on it.
doesNotCountWhen: The defect is corrected, bounded, or independently outweighed by reliable corroborating evidence.

fallacies.name: Sunk-cost fallacy
fallacies.summary: It continues an endeavor because resources already spent would otherwise be wasted, rather than because future benefits justify continuing.
fallacies.body: It continues an endeavor because resources already spent would otherwise be wasted, rather than because future benefits justify continuing. Past costs are unrecoverable and should not determine the best future choice.

examples.text: We must finish the failing film because we have already spent five million dollars on it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The main reason for continuation is money, time, or effort already expended rather than prospective costs and benefits.
doesNotCountWhen: Past investment is relevant only as evidence about future returns or when a recoverable commitment changes the options.

fallacies.name: Suppressed evidence
fallacies.summary: It reaches a conclusion by omitting known evidence that would materially weaken or qualify it.
fallacies.body: It reaches a conclusion by omitting known evidence that would materially weaken or qualify it. A selectively incomplete case can look decisive while hiding the information needed for proper evaluation.

examples.text: The prosecutor presents the eyewitness identification but omits that the witness later said the suspect was not present.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The arguer knows of relevant contrary evidence and withholds it while presenting the conclusion as complete.
doesNotCountWhen: The evidence is immaterial, legally excluded for a stated reason, or disclosed and addressed elsewhere.

fallacies.name: Taboo argument
fallacies.summary: Treating the prohibition or social unacceptability of discussing a claim as proof that the claim is false.
fallacies.body: Treating the prohibition or social unacceptability of discussing a claim as proof that the claim is false. A community can have practical reasons to limit discussion without establishing a factual verdict. This nonstandard rhetoric label concerns using the taboo itself as epistemic evidence.

examples.text: No respectable person discusses that hypothesis here, so it must be false.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A social prohibition on considering a proposition is offered as its refutation.
doesNotCountWhen: Declining a discussion because it is abusive or irrelevant does not itself assert that every proposition involved is false.

fallacies.name: Texas-sharpshooter fallacy
fallacies.summary: It selects a pattern after inspecting many data points and then treats that selected pattern as a preplanned discovery.
fallacies.body: It selects a pattern after inspecting many data points and then treats that selected pattern as a preplanned discovery. Post hoc clustering or target drawing makes chance patterns look evidential.

examples.text: After testing 100 stocks, an analyst highlights the seven that rose together and calls the group a predictive sector.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The target, subgroup, or comparison is chosen after seeing the data without accounting for the search.
doesNotCountWhen: The pattern and analysis were specified beforehand or corrected statistically for multiple comparisons.

fallacies.name: There-is-no-alternative fallacy
fallacies.summary: Claiming one policy is compulsory by excluding feasible alternatives without examining them.
fallacies.body: Claiming one policy is compulsory by excluding feasible alternatives without examining them. The move is a policy-focused false dilemma when the claimed absence of alternatives is unsupported. Constraints may narrow the options, but they need to be shown rather than used to foreclose comparison.

examples.text: We must close every local office because the only other option is bankruptcy, although shared premises and reduced hours have not been evaluated.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A preferred policy is declared uniquely feasible without supporting the exclusion of relevant alternatives.
doesNotCountWhen: A genuine constraint can leave only one feasible option after the alternatives have been assessed.

fallacies.name: Tokenism
fallacies.summary: It uses a token member or symbolic gesture to claim genuine inclusion, fairness, or representation without substantive change.
fallacies.body: It uses a token member or symbolic gesture to claim genuine inclusion, fairness, or representation without substantive change. One representative does not establish equal power, access, treatment, or outcomes.

examples.text: The board appoints one disabled adviser without voting rights and claims the company is fully accessible.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A token presence is offered as sufficient proof of equality while decision power or structural barriers remain unchanged.
doesNotCountWhen: The person has meaningful authority and broader evidence supports the claimed inclusion.

fallacies.name: Traitorous-critic fallacy
fallacies.summary: It dismisses criticism by accusing the critic of betrayal or disloyalty instead of addressing the criticism.
fallacies.body: It dismisses criticism by accusing the critic of betrayal or disloyalty instead of addressing the criticism. A critic's allegiance does not determine whether the objection is correct.

examples.text: You cannot object to our party's budget; doing so helps the enemy, so your objection is false.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response attacks the critic's loyalty or identity and provides no relevant answer to the substantive point.
doesNotCountWhen: Evidence shows the criticism is factually wrong or conflicts with a genuinely relevant duty, and that reason is stated.

fallacies.name: Treating nonsignificance as proof of no effect
fallacies.summary: It treats a non-significant statistical result as proof that the effect is exactly zero or absent.
fallacies.body: It treats a non-significant statistical result as proof that the effect is exactly zero or absent. Failure to reject a null hypothesis can reflect low power, imprecision, or a small effect.

examples.text: The trial found no statistically significant benefit, so the drug has no benefit at all.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion says no effect is established solely because a p-value crossed a significance threshold in the non-significant direction.
doesNotCountWhen: A sufficiently precise equivalence or non-inferiority analysis supports the bounded no-effect claim.

fallacies.name: Treating zero observed events as zero risk
fallacies.summary: It infers zero underlying risk from observing zero events in a finite sample.
fallacies.body: It infers zero underlying risk from observing zero events in a finite sample. Unobserved events remain possible, and the upper uncertainty bound depends on sample size and design.

examples.text: No tested circuit failed in 20 trials, so this circuit can never fail.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A finite zero count is converted into an absolute zero probability without a justified statistical bound or mechanism.
doesNotCountWhen: A proven physical impossibility or a valid confidence bound is stated with its uncertainty rather than absolute certainty.

fallacies.name: Trivial objections
fallacies.summary: It treats a minor defect or peripheral objection as if it defeated the central claim.
fallacies.body: It treats a minor defect or peripheral objection as if it defeated the central claim. A small error can reduce precision without invalidating the main argument or conclusion.

examples.text: The report misspells one city, so its independently verified climate measurements must all be false.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The objection concerns a nonessential detail but is used to reject the whole position.
doesNotCountWhen: The detail is material to the inference, or the conclusion explicitly depends on its accuracy.

fallacies.name: Tu quoque
fallacies.summary: It answers an accusation or argument by alleging that the accuser or opponent behaves inconsistently.
fallacies.body: It answers an accusation or argument by alleging that the accuser or opponent behaves inconsistently. Hypocrisy may affect credibility but does not make the original claim false.

examples.text: The mayor should not oppose bribery because she accepted a bribe last year.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response points to the opponent's conduct as the reason to reject the proposition instead of addressing its merits.
doesNotCountWhen: The opponent's conduct directly bears on a factual claim about their behavior or on a relevant credibility assessment.

fallacies.name: Two wrongs make a right
fallacies.summary: It concludes that one wrong action is permissible because another wrong action occurred.
fallacies.body: It concludes that one wrong action is permissible because another wrong action occurred. A prior injustice does not by itself create permission to commit a second injustice.

examples.text: The contractor cheated us, so we may steal its equipment without paying.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The sole justification for the proposed wrongdoing is a separate wrongdoing by another party.
doesNotCountWhen: A lawful remedy, necessity defense, proportional self-defense, or other independent justification applies.

fallacies.name: Type–token fallacy
fallacies.summary: It confuses a general kind or class with an individual instance of that kind.
fallacies.body: It confuses a general kind or class with an individual instance of that kind. Properties of a type need not belong to each token, and one token does not exhaust the type.

examples.text: The word "tree" has four letters, so every tree has four letters.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument transfers a linguistic or abstract property between a class and one of its members.
doesNotCountWhen: The predicate is explicitly about the type or explicitly about the token, with the distinction preserved.

fallacies.name: Undistributed middle
fallacies.summary: It uses a middle term that is not distributed in either premise to infer a relation between the end terms.
fallacies.body: It uses a middle term that is not distributed in either premise to infer a relation between the end terms. Sharing a category does not establish that two subjects are identical or related in the required way.

examples.text: All cats are mammals; all dogs are mammals; therefore, all dogs are cats.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: In a categorical syllogism, the middle term refers to only part of its class in both premises.
doesNotCountWhen: The middle term is distributed in at least one premise or additional premises establish the conclusion.

fallacies.name: Unfalsifiable defense
fallacies.summary: It protects a claim from criticism by adding conditions that make no possible observation count against it.
fallacies.body: It protects a claim from criticism by adding conditions that make no possible observation count against it. A defense that cannot be tested cannot distinguish the claim from alternatives by evidence.

examples.text: The medicine works for everyone, but any patient who shows no improvement was secretly not receptive to it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Every counterexample is reclassified as an exception without an independently testable rule.
doesNotCountWhen: The claim has specified disconfirming conditions and the exception rule is independently supported.

fallacies.name: Unreasonable inclusion
fallacies.summary: It includes a case in a category despite its failing the category's relevant defining criteria.
fallacies.body: It includes a case in a category despite its failing the category's relevant defining criteria. Classification by irrelevant resemblance distorts the scope and conclusions of the category.

examples.text: The museum counts a plastic toy as an ancient artifact because both are small objects on display.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The inclusion relies on a superficial feature while excluding a necessary or purpose-defining criterion.
doesNotCountWhen: The category is intentionally broad and the inclusion satisfies its stated operational definition.

fallacies.name: Unrepresentative generalization
fallacies.summary: It generalizes from a sample whose composition differs materially from the population about which the conclusion is made.
fallacies.body: It generalizes from a sample whose composition differs materially from the population about which the conclusion is made. Even a large sample can mislead when selection excludes or overweights relevant subgroups.

examples.text: A survey of private-school parents finds that all families support tuition increases, so all residents support them.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The sampled cases are selected or distributed in a way that cannot support the target population claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Probability sampling, weighting, or a justified transport argument makes the sample relevant to the target population.

fallacies.name: Unsupported conspiracy explanation
fallacies.summary: It explains an event by coordinated secret action without adequate evidence that the alleged conspiracy exists or caused it.
fallacies.body: It explains an event by coordinated secret action without adequate evidence that the alleged conspiracy exists or caused it. A conspiracy is a complex hypothesis requiring evidence of actors, coordination, means, and causal impact.

examples.text: The blackout happened because officials secretly switched off every substation to hide election fraud, although no records or witnesses support this.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The explanation adds hidden coordinated agents to resolve anomalies while treating missing evidence as expected secrecy.
doesNotCountWhen: Independent evidence establishes the actors, coordination, mechanism, and comparative advantage over simpler explanations.

fallacies.name: Unsupported counterfactual
fallacies.summary: It asserts what would have happened under a different condition without evidence or a justified causal model.
fallacies.body: It asserts what would have happened under a different condition without evidence or a justified causal model. An unobserved alternative outcome cannot be known merely by imagining it.

examples.text: If the city had rejected the tram, traffic would certainly have fallen because drivers would have adapted.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A claim about an unobserved alternative is stated with confidence but lacks a model, comparison, or relevant evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A credible causal design, historical comparison, or well-supported model identifies the counterfactual and uncertainty.

fallacies.name: Unwarranted contrast
fallacies.summary: It infers a meaningful contrast between two cases from their juxtaposition without establishing that the contrast exists.
fallacies.body: It infers a meaningful contrast between two cases from their juxtaposition without establishing that the contrast exists. Different descriptions or circumstances do not by themselves imply a causal, normative, or statistical difference.

examples.text: The report says rural patients improved while urban patients improved after treatment, so the treatment works only in rural areas.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument treats parallel wording or a named difference as evidence for a substantive difference without comparison data.
doesNotCountWhen: The contrast is defined in advance and supported by appropriate measurements, controls, or relevant premises.

fallacies.name: Use–mention error
fallacies.summary: It confuses an expression with the thing or concept that the expression denotes.
fallacies.body: It confuses an expression with the thing or concept that the expression denotes. Words, names, and quoted symbols are not identical to their referents.

examples.text: The name "Venus" has five letters, so the planet Venus has five letters.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A predicate true of the written or spoken expression is transferred to the object named by that expression, or vice versa.
doesNotCountWhen: Quotation and reference are explicitly distinguished, so the predicate's target is clear.

fallacies.name: We-have-to-do-something fallacy
fallacies.summary: Inferring that a particular action is justified merely because some action is needed.
fallacies.body: Inferring that a particular action is justified merely because some action is needed. Urgency establishes a reason to seek an effective response, not a reason to accept the first available intervention. The proposed action still needs a connection to the problem and an assessment of likely consequences.

examples.text: We must reduce accidents. This publicity campaign is something we can do. Therefore it will solve the accident problem.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A need for action and the availability of an action are used to justify that action without the missing effectiveness premise.
doesNotCountWhen: An urgent intervention can be justified by the best available evidence despite uncertainty and limited time.

fallacies.name: Weak man
fallacies.summary: It refutes an opponent's position by replacing it with a less defensible version that may retain only a vague resemblance.
fallacies.body: It refutes an opponent's position by replacing it with a less defensible version that may retain only a vague resemblance. A weakened substitute does not test the actual argument and can create a false victory.

examples.text: A scientist says emissions should be reduced gradually, and the reply says she wants to shut down all factories tomorrow.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The opponent's position is made more extreme, simplistic, or careless than the stated or strongest reasonable version.
doesNotCountWhen: The reconstruction preserves the original claim's scope and qualifications before criticism.

fallacies.name: Whataboutism
fallacies.summary: It deflects criticism by pointing to another person's alleged wrongdoing instead of addressing the criticism.
fallacies.body: It deflects criticism by pointing to another person's alleged wrongdoing instead of addressing the criticism. Another wrongdoing may be relevant to consistency or comparative policy, but it does not answer whether the original conduct was wrong.

examples.text: Asked why our company dumped waste illegally, the manager replies that a competitor also pollutes.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response changes from the original allegation to a comparable allegation without resolving the original issue.
doesNotCountWhen: The comparison is directly relevant to a stated consistency, enforcement, or causal question and the original issue is also addressed.

fallacies.name: Wishful thinking
fallacies.summary: It treats a desired outcome as evidence that the outcome is true or will occur.
fallacies.body: It treats a desired outcome as evidence that the outcome is true or will occur. Desire can bias assessment but cannot establish facts or probabilities.

examples.text: We want the merger to succeed, so regulators will approve it despite the missing filing.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion is supported chiefly by hope, preference, or confidence rather than evidence about the world.
doesNotCountWhen: The desired outcome is supported by independent evidence, and optimism is explicitly treated as motivation rather than proof.

fallacies.name: Worst-negates-the-bad fallacy
aliases: be grateful for what you have
fallacies.summary: Dismissing a real problem solely because a worse problem exists or is imaginable.
fallacies.body: Dismissing a real problem solely because a worse problem exists or is imaginable. A comparison with a worse condition can provide perspective without refuting the original complaint. Whether the problem deserves action depends on its own severity, remedies, and opportunity costs.

examples.text: Your apartment has no working heat, but some people have no home, so the broken heating is not a problem.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A problem's existence or significance is denied on the sole ground that another situation is worse.
doesNotCountWhen: Comparative severity is relevant when allocating scarce resources among competing urgent needs.

fallacies.name: Zero-tolerance fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming that eliminating every instance of a harm justifies any cost or response.
fallacies.body: Assuming that eliminating every instance of a harm justifies any cost or response. This rhetoric label concerns ignoring proportionality and alternative ways to reduce risk. A worthwhile aim does not by itself establish that unlimited expenditure or punishment is warranted.

examples.text: One minor reporting error is intolerable, so every employee must undergo an hour-long audit before sending any message.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Zero occurrence is treated as overriding all other relevant costs and constraints without justification.
doesNotCountWhen: A strict rule can be justified for a narrowly defined high-severity risk when proportionate and effective.
